teile.einleitung: The koala lives in the eucalyptus forests of Australia. It looks like a small bear, but is a marsupial. Koalas sleep a great deal because their food supplies little energy.
wichtigste: Koalas live only in the east and south-east of Australia.
The koala is not a bear, but a marsupial.
It eats eucalyptus leaves and gets most of its water from them.
Koalas sleep and doze for up to 20 hours a day.
Their fingerprints resemble those of humans.
With sharp claws they hold on to the branches.

abschnitte.text: The **koala** is sometimes called the **koala bear**, but it is not a bear. It is a **marsupial**, like the kangaroo. Its young grow up in a **pouch** on the mother’s belly. The dense, soft **fur** is grey to greyish brown, lighter on the belly. Koalas have round ears with long hairs and a big, dark nose.

Koalas live only in the **east and south-east of Australia**. They spend almost their whole life in **trees**. They come to the ground mostly only to go to the next tree. On their strong paws they have **sharp claws**. With these they cling securely to trunks and branches.

Koalas eat almost only **eucalyptus leaves**. These contain few nutrients and are hard to digest. For many other animals they are even poisonous. Koalas **drink** only rarely, because most of the water is in the moist leaves.

Because their food supplies so little **energy**, koalas save their strength. They sleep and doze for up to **20 hours** a day. They like best to sit comfortably in the **fork of a branch**. They are active mainly at dusk and at night.

Koalas have **fingerprints** that are very similar to those of humans. This is very rare in animals. Even under the microscope they are hard to tell apart. Today koalas are **endangered** in parts of Australia, for example through bushfires and the felling of their forests.

gewusst: Koala fingerprints look so much like human ones that they are hard to tell apart.
Koalas drink so rarely that people used to believe they never drank.

teile.einleitung: The Maldives are an island nation in the Indian Ocean, south-west of India. They consist of many small coral islands and are regarded as the flattest country in the world.
wichtigste: The Maldives lie in the Indian Ocean south-west of India.
They consist of about 1,200 islands, and only about 200 are inhabited.
The capital is called Malé.
The islands were formed from corals and make up atolls.
The Maldives are the flattest country in the world and the smallest country in Asia.
Rising sea levels threaten the islands.

abschnitte.text: The Maldives lie in the **Indian Ocean**, south-west of the southern tip of **India**. Sri Lanka is not far away either. The country consists of about **1,200** small islands, but people live on only about 200 of them. In terms of area, the Maldives are the smallest country in **Asia**. The water is warm all year round.

The islands were formed from **coral reefs** and coral sand. That is why the beaches are so white. Many islands lie in ring-shaped groups, the **atolls**. An atoll is a ring of reefs and islands with a shallow **lagoon** in the middle. By the way, the word atoll comes from the language of the Maldives.

The capital, **Malé**, lies on a small island that is almost completely built over with houses. A large part of the country's population lives there. The streets are narrow, and there is hardly any free space. The airport lies on an island of its own nearby.

The most important branch of the economy is **tourism**. Many guests come because of the beaches, the clear water and the reefs for diving and snorkelling. Often there is only a single hotel on an island. **Fishing** is also important, especially the catching of tuna.

Most of the islands rise only one or two metres above the sea. No other country is so flat. If the **sea level** rises because of global warming, islands can be flooded. This threatens houses, drinking water and fields. That is why the Maldives campaign strongly for **climate protection** internationally.

gewusst: The word “atoll” is one of the few words that have passed from the language of the Maldives into many languages of the world.
The highest natural point in the Maldives is only a few metres above the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Laguna del Carbón is a salt lake in Patagonia in the south of Argentina. It lies about 105 metres below sea level and is the lowest point in South America.
wichtigste: The Laguna del Carbón lies in the Argentine province of Santa Cruz.
It lies about 105 metres below sea level.
It is the lowest point in South America.
It is also the lowest point in the Southern and Western Hemispheres.
The lake lies in a basin with no outflow.

abschnitte.text: The **Laguna del Carbón** lies in the province of **Santa Cruz** in **Patagonia**, not far from the Atlantic coast. Its surface lies about **105 metres below sea level**. That makes it the lowest point in South America and even in the whole **Southern and Western Hemispheres**. The lowest point in North America, in Death Valley, lies only about 86 metres below sea level.

abschnitte.titel: A salt lake in a basin
abschnitte.text: The lake lies in a **basin with no outflow**. This means that water flows in, but no river carries it out again. The water evaporates in the dry, windy landscape. The dissolved salts are left behind. That is why the Laguna del Carbón is a **salt lake**, with white crusts of salt often lying on its shore.

The lowest point on land on the whole Earth is the shore of the **Dead Sea** in western Asia, more than 400 metres below sea level. The lowest point in **Switzerland**, on the other hand, is Lake Maggiore in Ticino, about 193 metres **above** sea level. As you can see, even in places far below sea level there does not have to be any seawater if the land is cut off from the sea.

gewusst: Although it lies below sea level, the Laguna del Carbón is not connected to the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Strait of Magellan is a narrow channel at the southern tip of South America. It separates the mainland from the island of Tierra del Fuego and links the Atlantic with the Pacific.
wichtigste: The Strait of Magellan separates the South American mainland from Tierra del Fuego.
It lies almost entirely in Chile.
It links the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific Ocean.
Ferdinand Magellan sailed through it in 1520 as the first European.
The Drake Passage lies further south, between Cape Horn and Antarctica.

abschnitte.text: **Ferdinand Magellan** was a Portuguese navigator in the service of Spain. In 1519 he set out with several ships to find a sea route west to the Spice Islands. In **1520** he found a strait at the southern tip of South America and sailed through it as the first European. It was named the **Strait of Magellan** after him. Magellan himself died in 1521 in the Philippines, but part of his crew completed the first **circumnavigation of the world**.

The Strait of Magellan lies almost entirely in **Chile**. To the south lies the big island of **Tierra del Fuego**. The strait is winding and in places very narrow. The weather is often cold, windy and stormy. The biggest town on the strait is **Punta Arenas**. Further south, between **Cape Horn** and Antarctica, lies the much wider **Drake Passage**.

For a long time the Strait of Magellan was an important route for ships between the Atlantic and the Pacific. It was more sheltered than the dangerous voyage round Cape Horn. Since the **Panama Canal** opened in 1914, many ships prefer to sail through there. Even so, ships still use the Strait of Magellan today.

gewusst: Tierra del Fuego, which means “Land of Fire”, got its name because Magellan's men saw many fires of the local people on the coast.
Of Magellan's five ships, only one returned to Spain.

teile.einleitung: On a cruise, people travel on a big ship from port to port. They usually sleep and eat on board. Cruises are very popular, but they are also criticised because of exhaust fumes and mass tourism.
wichtigste: In 2024, according to the industry association CLIA, around 34.6 million people took an ocean cruise.
The Caribbean is the most important cruising region in the world.
When it entered service in 2024, the Icon of the Seas was the largest cruise ship in the world.
Many ships sail under flags of convenience, for example those of Panama, the Bahamas or Malta.
Shore power in port reduces exhaust fumes and noise.
In Antarctica, no more than 100 people may be ashore at a landing site at the same time.

abschnitte.text: A **cruise ship** is like a hotel on the water. It has cabins, restaurants, swimming pools and theatres. The ship sails on during the night, and during the day the guests visit a town on land. The ships keep getting bigger. When it entered service in 2024, the **Icon of the Seas**, owned by the shipping company Royal Caribbean, was the largest cruise ship in the world. It is about 365 metres long and has room for more than 7,000 passengers.

According to the industry association **CLIA**, around **34.6 million** people took an ocean cruise in 2024. That was a record and clearly more than in 2019, before the pandemic. The most important cruising region is the **Caribbean**. It is close to the big North American market and has warm weather all year round. **Miami** in Florida is an important port of departure. The **Mediterranean** and northern Europe are also popular.

Many cruise ships are registered in countries such as **Panama**, the **Bahamas** or **Malta**. These are called **flags of convenience**. The shipping companies pay less tax there and have lower costs, for example in terms of **employment law** for the crew. Critics find this unfair, while the shipping companies point out that international rules still apply.

Without **shore power**, the diesel generators keep running in port too and pollute the air of the city. With shore power, ships take electricity from the land and switch off their engines. New ships often run on **liquefied natural gas**, or **LNG** for short. It produces less sulphur and soot than **heavy fuel oil**, but it is still a fossil fuel. People also criticise the **methane slip**, because methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Port cities often benefit little, because the guests eat and sleep on board, but they fill the old towns to bursting.

The shipping company **MSC**, which owns **MSC Cruises**, has its headquarters in **Geneva**. River cruises are also popular in Switzerland, for example on the **Rhine** from **Basel**. In **Antarctica** particularly strict rules apply. Under the rules of the association **IAATO**, no more than 100 people may be ashore at a landing site at the same time. Ships with more than 500 passengers may not make any landings at all.

gewusst: Big cruise ships sometimes have water slides, climbing walls and even ice rinks.
Cruise guests often stay ashore for only a few hours.

teile.einleitung: The Congo Conference took place in Berlin in 1884 and 1885. There European powers laid down rules for how they could claim territories in Africa. Africans were not represented.
wichtigste: The Congo Conference met in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885.
It was convened by the German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, together with France.
Participants were European states, the USA and the Ottoman Empire, but no Africans.
The result was the General Act with the principle of effective occupation.
The Belgian king Leopold II received the Congo Free State as his personal property.
The conference accelerated the race for Africa.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many European states wanted **colonies** in Africa. To avoid quarrels among themselves, Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck**, together with France, invited them to a conference in **Berlin**. It lasted from November 1884 to February 1885. Participants were European states, the **USA** and the **Ottoman Empire**. **African rulers** were not invited. Africa was negotiated over without Africans.

In the end the participants signed the **General Act of the Berlin Conference**. Among other things it regulated free trade in the Congo Basin and free navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers. Important was the principle of **effective occupation**. A claim to a coastal area counted only if a power actually administered it and informed the other states. This **principle of effectiveness** drove the states to occupy territories as quickly as possible.

The Belgian king **Leopold II** had already acquired territories on the Congo earlier. The participants recognised the **Congo Free State** as his **personal property**. Under his rule people were forced to work, above all to collect rubber. Very many people died. After fierce criticism the Belgian state took over the territory as a colony in 1908. Only in 1960 did the Congo become independent.

After the conference the division of Africa went very fast. People speak of the **Scramble for Africa**. Around 1914 only two states were no longer under European rule: **Ethiopia**, which repelled an Italian attack at **Adwa** in 1896, and **Liberia**, which had been independent since 1847. Many borders were drawn with a ruler on maps, without regard for the peoples on the spot.

Some of the borders of that time still exist. One example is the **Caprivi Strip** in Namibia. Through a treaty between Germany and Great Britain in 1890, the colony of German South West Africa received a narrow access to the **Zambezi** River. The strip is named after Chancellor **Leo von Caprivi**.

gewusst: At the conference Africa was not divided directly, but the rules for doing so were laid down.
The Congo Free State was about eighty times as big as Belgium.

teile.einleitung: Kuala Lumpur is the capital of Malaysia in South-East Asia. The city is known for its huge skyscrapers, its many cultures and its warm, humid tropical climate.
wichtigste: Kuala Lumpur is the capital of Malaysia.
The name means “muddy river mouth”.
The Petronas Towers are 452 metres tall and were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
Since 2023, Merdeka 118 has been the tallest building in Malaysia.
Many government offices have moved to the planned city of Putrajaya.
Near the city lie the Batu Caves with a Hindu shrine.

abschnitte.text: The name **Kuala Lumpur** comes from the Malay language. “Kuala” means river mouth, and “lumpur” means mud. The city grew up in the 19th century where two muddy rivers flow together. At that time many workers came to mine **tin** in the area. In time, the small settlement became a big city.

The **Petronas Towers** are two identical towers, known as twin towers. They are 452 metres tall and were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004. A bridge high up in the air joins the two towers. Since 2023, the skyscraper **Merdeka 118** has been the tallest building in Malaysia. It is almost 680 metres tall, and only the Burj Khalifa in Dubai is taller.

Kuala Lumpur is the **capital** of Malaysia. However, many ministries and offices have moved to the newly built planned city of **Putrajaya** to the south. A planned city is built on open land according to a finished plan. Parliament and the king still have their seat in Kuala Lumpur.

abschnitte.titel: Many cultures and the Batu Caves
abschnitte.text: The people who live in Kuala Lumpur are mainly **Malays**, **Chinese** and **Indians**. That is why there are mosques, Chinese temples and Hindu temples, and you can try food from many cuisines. North of the city lie the **Batu Caves**, large limestone caves with a Hindu shrine. In front of the entrance stands a huge golden statue of the god **Murugan**, and a long, colourful staircase leads up to it.

gewusst: The staircase to the Batu Caves has 272 steps.
From 1998 to 2004, the tallest buildings in the world were not in the USA but in Kuala Lumpur.

teile.einleitung: Life expectancy states how many years people live on average. It is an important measure of how good health, nutrition and living conditions are in a country.
wichtigste: Life expectancy at birth shows how long a newborn baby would live on average.
Remaining life expectancy gives the years left from a certain age.
Worldwide, life expectancy around 2023 was about 73 years, according to the UN.
In the past, it was mainly high child mortality that caused low figures.
In Africa south of the Sahara, life expectancy is lowest today.
Switzerland and Japan are among the countries with the highest life expectancy.

abschnitte.text: **Life expectancy at birth** shows how many years a newborn baby would live on average if today's death rates stayed the same. So it is an average and not a prediction for any one person. **Remaining life expectancy** shows how many years, for example, a 65-year-old person still has ahead of them on average. It is important for planning old-age provision, in Switzerland for example for the **AVS** (old-age insurance).

In earlier centuries, life expectancy was much lower. The most important reason was high **child mortality**: many children died before their fifth birthday. This pulled the average down sharply, although adults often reached 60 or 70 years of age. Around 1950, the world's life expectancy was below 50 years. According to the UN, around 2023 it was about **73 years**.

There are big differences between countries. Life expectancy is lowest in **Africa south of the Sahara**, where in countries such as Nigeria, Chad or Lesotho it is under 60 years. The reasons are infectious diseases, poverty and weak health systems. In general: the higher the **prosperity**, the higher the life expectancy. The **Preston curve** shows this link, which flattens out at high incomes.

abschnitte.titel: Top of the table: Switzerland and Japan
abschnitte.text: **Japan**, **Switzerland**, Monaco and Hong Kong have led the rankings for years. In Japan, women live to be over 87 on average. Good nutrition, hygiene, clean water and good health care all contribute. Safe workplaces and fewer accidents also play a part.

Women live longer than men in almost all countries. One reason is that men, on average, smoke more, drink more alcohol and have more accidents. Biological factors also play a part. Crises can lower life expectancy: during the **Covid-19 pandemic** in 2020 and 2021 it fell temporarily in many countries, because many older people in particular died.

gewusst: Around 1950, the world's life expectancy was still below 50 years.
Life expectancy is an average: in the past, too, many adults grew old.

teile.einleitung: Air pressure is the weight of the air pressing down on us and on the Earth's surface. It is very important for the weather, because differences in air pressure create wind.
wichtigste: At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1,013 hectopascals.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer.
Wind basically blows from high to low pressure.
The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure is.
A high often brings fine weather, and a low often brings changeable weather.

abschnitte.text: The Earth is surrounded by a shell of air, the **atmosphere**. Air has weight too. It presses on us from all sides, but we do not feel it because our body pushes back. The average air pressure at sea level is **1,013.25 hectopascals**, abbreviated hPa. Values above this count as fairly high, and values below it as fairly low.

Air pressure is measured with a **barometer**. The Italian **Evangelista Torricelli** invented the mercury barometer in the 17th century. Today there are aneroid barometers and electronic sensors, even in many mobile phones. When air pressure rises, the weather often gets better. When it falls fast, bad weather often follows.

On weather maps you can see **high-pressure areas** and **low-pressure areas**. Air flows from the area of high pressure to the area of low pressure to even out the difference. This is how **wind** arises. The bigger the difference, the stronger it blows. A high often brings dry, sunny weather, and a low often brings clouds and rain.

The higher you climb, the less air lies above you. That is why **air pressure falls with height**. On the **Jungfraujoch** it is clearly lower than in Zurich. At a height of about 5,500 metres it is only about half as great as at sea level. That is why breathing becomes harder at great heights, and water boils below 100 degrees.

gewusst: A packet of crisps puffs up when you take it up a high mountain.
Aeroplane cabins are artificially pressurised so that the passengers can breathe easily.

teile.einleitung: Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa. It stands in Tanzania in East Africa and is a volcano. On its summit lie snow and ice, although it is hot below.
wichtigste: At 5,895 metres, Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.
It is a volcano with the three cones Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.
The highest point is called Uhuru Peak and lies on Kibo.
In 1889 Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller were the first to reach the summit.
The glaciers on the summit have been melting for many years.
Around the mountain lies savanna with elephants.

abschnitte.text: **Kilimanjaro** stands in **Tanzania** in East Africa, near the border with Kenya. Its highest point lies at **5,895 metres**. That makes it higher than any mountain in the Alps, including Mont Blanc and the Dufourspitze. It rises on its own out of the flat landscape and can therefore be seen from far away.

Kilimanjaro is a **volcano**. It consists of three volcanic cones: **Kibo**, **Mawenzi** and **Shira**. Kibo is the highest. On it lies **Uhuru Peak**. “Uhuru” means “freedom” in the Swahili language. The volcano has not erupted for a very long time.

Up on the mountain it is very cold. That is why **snow** and **glaciers** lie there, although it is hot on the plain. The glaciers, however, have been getting **smaller and smaller** for many years. Experts expect that they could disappear completely within a few decades.

In **1889** the German geographer **Hans Meyer** from Leipzig and the Austrian mountaineer **Ludwig Purtscheller** were the first to reach the summit. For Meyer it was already the third attempt. Today many people climb the mountain every year. It takes several days, so that the body can get used to the thin air.

At the foot of Kilimanjaro lies **savanna**. There are national parks there in which, for example, **elephants** live. Higher up follow rainforest, heath and finally bare rocky desert. Anyone climbing the mountain thus walks through several landscapes.

gewusst: On the way to the summit of Kilimanjaro you pass through almost all the climate zones, from hot to icy.
Since 1987 Kilimanjaro National Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: Land and sea breezes are winds on coasts and big lakes that change direction over the course of a day. They arise because land and water heat up and cool down at different speeds.
wichtigste: Land heats up faster than water and also cools down faster.
During the day the sea breeze blows from the water to the land.
At night the land breeze blows from the land to the water.
The wind arises because warm air rises and cooler air flows in.
Such winds also occur on big lakes such as Lake Geneva.

abschnitte.text: When the sun shines, the **land** heats up much faster than the **water**. Above the warm land the air also becomes warm. Warm air is lighter and **rises**. So that no gap is left, cooler air flows in from the water. This is how the **sea breeze** blows from the sea to the land during the day on the coast. On hot days it brings pleasant cooling to the beach.

At night it is the other way round. The land **cools down faster** than the water, which stores heat for a long time. Now the air above the water is warmer and rises. The cooler air from the land flows out over the water. This is the **land breeze**. In the past, fishermen used it to sail out in their boats in the early morning.

Land and sea breezes do not occur only by the sea. On big **lakes** such as Lake Geneva or Lake Constance, too, the winds change direction on fine summer days. Sailors and windsurfers watch out for this. In the mountains there is something similar: the **mountain and valley breeze**. By day it blows up the valley, and at night down the valley.

gewusst: Land and sea breezes arise mainly in calm, sunny weather, when no strong wind of another kind is blowing.

teile.einleitung: A climate diagram shows at a glance how warm and how wet it is at a place over the year. Especially well known is the style of diagram by Walter and Lieth. With it you can even read off which months are dry.
wichtigste: Blue columns show the precipitation per month.
The red line shows the mean monthly temperature.
In Walter and Lieth, 10 °C corresponds exactly to 20 mm of precipitation.
If the temperature curve lies above the precipitation, the month is arid.
The annual range is the difference between the warmest and the coldest month.
If January is the warmest month, the place is probably in the Southern Hemisphere.

abschnitte.text: On the horizontal axis stand the twelve **months**. The **blue columns** show how much **precipitation** falls on average per month, measured in millimetres. The **red line** joins the **mean monthly temperatures**. In this way you can see in which months it is warm or cold, wet or dry.

In the climate diagram by **Walter and Lieth** the axes are labelled in the ratio **1 to 2**. **10 °C** stands at the same height as **20 mm** of precipitation. So that very wet months do not burst the diagram, precipitation above 100 mm is reduced on a scale of **1 to 10**. This very wet, **perhumid** area is filled in black.

If the temperature curve lies **above** the precipitation, more water evaporates than falls from the sky. Such dry months are called **arid**, and the area is usually dotted or yellow. If the precipitation lies above, the month is **humid**. Example: at 15 °C a month would need at least 2 times 15 = 30 mm of precipitation. With only 25 mm it is arid.

abschnitte.titel: What else you can read off
abschnitte.text: The **annual range** is the difference between the warmest and the coldest month. If the warmest month has 19 °C and the coldest minus 1 °C, it is **20 °C**. If **January** is the warmest month, the place is probably in the **Southern Hemisphere**, because there it is summer in January. This applies, for example, to Sydney or Buenos Aires.

gewusst: The diagram by Walter and Lieth comes from two plant researchers who wanted to use it to compare the habitats of plants.
In the climate diagram of Zurich you can see that the most rain falls in summer.

teile.einleitung: Machu Picchu is an ancient ruined city of the Incas high in the Andes of Peru. It lies on a mountain ridge above a deep valley and is one of the most famous sights in the world.
wichtigste: The Incas built Machu Picchu around the year 1450, that is, in the 15th century.
The city lies at about 2,430 metres above sea level.
The name means “old mountain” or “old peak”.
In 1911 the American Hiram Bingham made Machu Picchu famous worldwide.
Since 1983 Machu Picchu has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Behind the ruins rises the pointed mountain Huayna Picchu.

abschnitte.text: **Machu Picchu** lies in **Peru** on a mountain ridge high above the valley of the Urubamba River. The city is at about **2,430 metres** above sea level, about as high as many Alpine peaks. Clouds often drift over the ruins. The name comes from the **Quechua** language and means **“old mountain”**. The pointed mountain behind it is called **Huayna Picchu**, “young mountain”.

The **Incas** built Machu Picchu around the year **1450**, in the 15th century. At that time they had a large empire in the **Andes**. Machu Picchu was probably a residence for a ruler and a religious place. About a hundred years later, the city was abandoned. The Spanish, who conquered the Inca Empire, apparently never found it.

The Incas were outstanding builders. The stones of many **temple walls** were cut so exactly that they hold together **without mortar**. Often not even a knife blade fits in between. On the steep slopes the Incas built **terraces**. On them they grew **maize** and **potatoes**, and the terraces protected the slope from slipping.

Farmers in the area had known the ruins for a long time. But Machu Picchu became known worldwide only in **1911**, when the American **Hiram Bingham** went there and reported on it. In **1983** Machu Picchu became both a **World Cultural Heritage Site and a World Natural Heritage Site**. In 2007 it was chosen as one of the “new seven wonders of the world”.

Today very many people visit the ruins. Many travel up by train and bus, while others hike along the old **Inca Trail**. **Llamas** roam freely between the old walls and keep the grass short. To protect the ruins, the number of visitors per day is limited.

gewusst: The Incas had no wheels for carts and no iron tools, yet they built walls like these.
The walls of Machu Picchu have survived many earthquakes.

teile.einleitung: The Llanos are wide grassy plains in South America. They lie in the area of the Orinoco River in Venezuela and Colombia and change greatly between the rainy season and the dry season.
wichtigste: The Llanos lie on the Orinoco in Venezuela and Colombia.
They are savannas, that is, grassland with scattered trees.
In the rainy season large areas are flooded.
In the dry season the land is parched and hot.
Many people there make their living from cattle farming.

abschnitte.text: The Spanish word **“llanos”** means plains. The Llanos stretch between the **Andes** and the **Orinoco** River. They are **savannas**: wide grassland with groups of trees and palms. Narrow strips of forest grow along the rivers.

The year is divided into two seasons. In the **rainy season** the rivers burst their banks, and huge areas lie under water. In the **dry season** hardly any rain falls, the grass turns brown and the ground becomes hard. Animals and people have to adapt to this change.

Many waterbirds, **caimans** and the **capybara**, the biggest rodent in the world, live in the Llanos. **Cattle farming** has been carried on there for centuries. The herders on horseback are called **llaneros**. Their culture, for example the music known as **joropo**, is very well known in Venezuela and Colombia.

gewusst: The capybara can swim and dive well.
Oil is also produced in the Llanos.

teile.einleitung: The Least Developed Countries, or LDCs for short, are the least developed countries in the world. The United Nations keeps a list of these countries so that they receive special support.
wichtigste: The UN has kept the category of Least Developed Countries since 1971.
Three criteria count: income, human assets and economic vulnerability.
At the end of 2024 the UN counted 44 countries as LDCs.
About three quarters of the LDCs are in Africa.
Haiti is the only LDC in the Americas.
Botswana was the first country to leave the category, in 1994.

abschnitte.text: The category was created in **1971** by the **United Nations**. The UN's **Committee for Development Policy** reviews the list every three years. It proposes which countries can be added or can leave the group. The countries on the list receive help, for example cheaper loans and advantages in trade.

Whether a country counts as an LDC depends on three criteria. First, **income**, measured as gross national income per head. Second, **human assets**: these include people's health, nutrition and education. Third, **economic vulnerability**, that is, how badly a country suffers from natural disasters or price swings. A country has to reach threshold values on several criteria to leave the list.

At the end of 2024, after the graduation of **São Tomé and Príncipe**, there were still **44** LDCs. About three quarters of them, 32 countries in all, lie in **Africa**. Others lie in Asia and the Pacific. In the Americas only **Haiti** is on the list. It is regarded as the poorest country in the Americas.

The first country to leave the category was **Botswana** in 1994, thanks to income from diamonds and a stable government. Other countries followed later, for example **Bhutan** in Asia in December 2023. Graduating is a success, but it also brings problems: after a transition period, **preferential tariffs** and cheap loans fall away. That is why there are transition strategies meant to make the change easier.

The UN regularly holds conferences on the least developed countries. The fifth conference took place in March 2023 in **Doha** in Qatar. There, the **Doha Programme of Action** for the years 2022 to 2031 was adopted. The conference before that was in Istanbul in 2011. Switzerland, too, supports many of these countries as part of its development cooperation.

gewusst: The list of LDCs is officially reviewed only every three years.
Before its graduation, Botswana was one of the poorest countries in Africa.

teile.einleitung: The Lithium Triangle is an area in South America where Argentina, Bolivia and Chile meet. Beneath its salt lakes lies a large share of the Earth's known lithium reserves.
wichtigste: The Lithium Triangle includes areas in Argentina, Bolivia and Chile.
Lithium is obtained there mainly from brine beneath salt lakes.
Sun and wind make the water evaporate in large pools.
The Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the biggest salt flat on Earth.
The main criticism is the high water use in a dry region.
The biggest lithium producer in 2023 was Australia, not a country in the Triangle.

abschnitte.text: The **Lithium Triangle** lies in the dry highlands of the **Andes**. Here **Argentina**, **Bolivia** and **Chile** meet. In this area there are many large salt flats, called **salars**. Well known are the **Salar de Uyuni** in Bolivia, with a good 10,000 square kilometres, and the **Salar de Atacama** in Chile.

Beneath the salars lies **brine**, a salt solution containing lithium. It is pumped up and run into large **evaporation pools**. In the dry, sunny high-altitude setting, **sun and wind** make the water evaporate over many months. When the solution is strong enough, soda is added. This produces **lithium carbonate**, a starting material for batteries.

With **direct lithium extraction**, or DLE for short, big evaporation pools are not needed. Special substances or membranes take the lithium directly out of the brine. The remaining brine can then be pumped back into the ground. The hope is to save water and time in this way.

The most frequent criticism is the high **water use** in one of the driest regions in the world. Pumping can lower the **water table**. As a result, wetlands, animals such as flamingos and the farming of **Indigenous communities** can suffer. Supporters, on the other hand, stress that lithium is important for electric cars and therefore for protecting the climate.

Although a great deal of lithium lies in the Triangle, **Australia** was the biggest producer in 2023. There, lithium is mainly obtained from the rock **spodumene**. **Chile** was in second place. Bolivia has huge reserves but produces little. In 2023 Chile decided on a national lithium strategy so that the state, through the company **Codelco**, would hold a majority in new projects.

gewusst: The Salar de Uyuni is so flat that after rain it looks like a gigantic mirror.
Lithium is the lightest metal and therefore ideal for light batteries.

teile.einleitung: Lava is liquid, glowing hot rock that reaches the Earth's surface in a volcanic eruption. When it cools, it turns into new, solid rock.
wichtigste: Inside the Earth, molten rock is called magma, and at the surface it is called lava.
Lava can be about 1,100 to 1,200 degrees Celsius hot.
Fresh lava glows red and orange, and when it has cooled it turns dark.
Cooled lava turns into rock such as basalt.
Pumice is so light that it floats, and obsidian is black volcanic glass.
Pahoehoe, aa and pillow lava are different forms of lava.

abschnitte.text: Deep inside the Earth it is so hot that rock melts. This liquid rock is called **magma**. In a volcanic eruption it rises upwards. As soon as it is at the Earth's surface, it is called **lava**. It flows down the mountain or is hurled into the air. Well-known volcanoes with lava include Etna and Stromboli in Italy or the volcanoes of Hawaii and Iceland.

Lava can be up to about **1,200 degrees Celsius** hot. **Basalt lava**, such as flows out in Hawaii or Iceland, is about 1,100 to 1,200 degrees hot. That is much hotter than an oven. Fresh lava therefore glows **red and orange**. When it cools, it turns dark and finally **solid**. New rock forms from it, for example **basalt**.

If lava cools very quickly, **obsidian** forms. This is a black, shiny volcanic glass with sharp edges. In the past, people made knives and arrowheads from it. **Pumice** is full of small air holes, because gases formed bubbles in the lava. That is why it is so light that it floats on water. It is also used to rub rough skin off the feet.

For two forms of lava, words from the language of **Hawaii** are used. **Pahoehoe** is smooth lava with a skin that folds into ridges like twisted ropes. **Aa** is rough, jagged lava full of sharp lumps. You can hardly walk on it barefoot. If lava flows out **under water**, its surface cools at once. Round lobes form, which are called **pillow lava**.

In Switzerland there are no active volcanoes today. Not far from Schaffhausen, though, lies the **Hegau** in southern Germany, with mountains that were once volcanoes. If you want to see lava up close, you have to travel to Italy or Iceland. Volcano researchers wear special protective suits there when they go close to flowing lava.

gewusst: Pillow lava shows geologists that a rock once formed in the sea.
New land can grow from lava: Hawaii and Iceland were formed by volcanoes.

teile.einleitung: The llama is a domestic animal from the Andes in South America. It is related to the camel but has no hump, and it is known for spitting when it is annoyed.
wichtigste: The llama comes from South America, mainly from the Andes.
It was bred long ago from the wild guanaco.
Llamas belong to the camel family but have no hump.
They carry loads and provide wool.
When they are annoyed, llamas spit.
The alpaca is smaller and has especially fine wool.

abschnitte.text: The **llama** comes from **South America**. Especially many llamas live in **Peru** and **Bolivia**, high up in the **Andes**. The people there have kept llamas for thousands of years. The llama was bred from the wild **guanaco**, which still lives in South America today. The Incas, too, used llamas as important helpers.

Llamas belong to the **camel** family. Because they come from the Americas, they are also called **New World camels**. Unlike camels, however, they have **no hump**, and their back is straight. On each foot, llamas have **two toes** with claws and soft soles. This lets them walk safely on stony mountain paths and spares the ground.

In the Andes, llamas are often used as **pack animals**. They carry goods along steep mountain paths where no car can go. If the load is too heavy, a llama simply lies down and refuses to go on. Their **wool** is made into warm clothes and blankets. The smaller **alpaca** is also related to the llama and is kept mainly for its especially soft wool.

Llamas **spit** when they are annoyed or feel threatened. Most of the time, though, they spit at other llamas, for example in a quarrel over food. Before that they often lay their ears back, which is a warning. People who treat them calmly and kindly are rarely spat at. In Switzerland, too, there are farms where you can go hiking with llamas or alpacas.

gewusst: Llamas like to live in groups and do not feel happy alone.
Llamas often leave their droppings together in a few fixed places.

teile.einleitung: Morocco is a kingdom in north-west Africa. It lies on the Atlantic and the Mediterranean and is separated from Spain only by a narrow strait.
wichtigste: Morocco is a kingdom with a king at its head.
The capital is Rabat, and the biggest city is Casablanca.
The Strait of Gibraltar separates Morocco from Spain.
Marrakesh is called “the Red City”, and Chefchaouen “the Blue City”.
A typical dish is the tagine.
In Fez stands al-Qarawiyyin, one of the oldest universities in the world.

abschnitte.text: Morocco lies in north-west Africa. In the west it has a long coast on the **Atlantic Ocean** with many surfing beaches, and in the north lies the Mediterranean. The **Strait of Gibraltar** separates Morocco from Spain, and at its narrowest point it is only about 14 kilometres wide. On the north coast lie the Spanish cities of **Ceuta** and **Melilla**, and their borders are external borders of the EU.

Morocco is a **kingdom**, and a king stands at the head of the state. The capital is **Rabat**, where the king lives and the government works. The biggest city is **Casablanca**, with a big port on the Atlantic. The languages spoken are mainly Arabic and Amazigh languages, and often French.

Many houses and walls in **Marrakesh** are built of reddish clay. That is why it is called “the Red City”. In **Chefchaouen** in the Rif mountains, many houses and alleys are painted light blue, and it is called “the Blue City”. In **Fez** stands the university **al-Qarawiyyin**, founded in the year 859. It is regarded as one of the oldest universities in the world that still exist.

A typical dish is the **tagine**. This is the name of a clay pot with a pointed lid and also of the stew cooked in it. Vegetables, meat and spices cook slowly in it. **Couscous** and sweet mint tea are also popular.

The **Atlas** mountains run through Morocco, and in winter there is often snow there. To the south of them, the **Sahara** begins, with sand dunes and oases. On the coast the climate is mild. So in one country there are beaches, mountains and desert.

gewusst: On clear days you can see from Morocco across the Strait of Gibraltar as far as Spain.
Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri.

teile.einleitung: Marco Polo was a merchant from Venice who travelled as far as China in the 13th century. His account of his journey made Asia known in Europe.
wichtigste: Marco Polo was born around 1254 in Venice.
In 1271 he set out for Asia with his father and his uncle.
He travelled to China along the Silk Road.
For many years he lived at the court of Kublai Khan.
In 1295, after about 24 years, he returned to Venice.
His account was written in a prison in Genoa and is called “Il Milione”.

abschnitte.text: **Marco Polo** was born around 1254 in the trading city of **Venice**. His father **Niccolò** and his uncle **Maffeo** were merchants and already knew the way to China. In 1271 they took young Marco with them on their second great journey to Asia.

The three travelled along the **Silk Road**. This was a network of caravan routes between the Mediterranean and China. They crossed deserts and mountains and were on the road for several years. Along these routes silk, spices and other valuable goods were traded.

abschnitte.titel: At the court of Kublai Khan
abschnitte.text: In China, Marco Polo came to the court of **Kublai Khan**. He was the Mongol Great Khan and ruled over China. Marco Polo served him for many years and travelled through the country on his behalf. He marvelled at many things, for example at **paper money**: in Europe people paid with coins, while in China they paid with printed paper.

In 1295, after about **24 years**, Marco Polo returned to Venice. Later he was taken prisoner in the war between Venice and Genoa. In the **prison in Genoa** he told his experiences to a fellow prisoner, **Rustichello da Pisa**, who wrote them down. The book is called **“Il Milione”** in Italian, and in English it is also known as “The Travels of Marco Polo”. It was widely read in Europe.

gewusst: Marco Polo was only about 17 years old when he set out for Asia.
His book was translated and copied into many languages as early as the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: Rural areas are everything that is not a city: villages, hamlets, farms, fields and woods. Life in the countryside looks a little different around the world, but much of it is similar.
wichtigste: In the countryside there is more space and there are fewer houses than in the city.
A village is a small settlement, and a hamlet is even smaller.
Many people in the countryside work in farming.
In Switzerland, an alp is a summer pasture in the mountains.
In poor countries, farmers sometimes still plough with oxen or buffalo.
When many people move from the countryside to the city, this is called rural depopulation.

abschnitte.text: A **village** is a small settlement in the countryside. There, many people know each other. A **hamlet** is even smaller, often with only a few farmhouses standing together. In the countryside the houses stand further apart than in the city. In between there are **fields**, **meadows** and **woods**.

In the countryside, many people work in **farming**. Farmers grow grain, vegetables or fruit and keep animals. In rich countries, tractors and machines help. In some poor countries, farmers cannot afford a tractor. Then strong animals such as **oxen** or **water buffalo** pull the plough.

Switzerland has something special: the **alp**. This is a **summer pasture** in the mountains. In summer, farmers take their cows up to it, which is called the **drive up to the alp**. Up there, the animals eat fresh grass, and the milk is often made into alpine cheese. In autumn they return to the valley in the **descent from the alp**.

abschnitte.titel: Life in the countryside around the world
abschnitte.text: In some villages in Africa and Asia there is no **running water** in the house. Then children and adults fetch water from the **well** and carry it home. In the west of the USA, **cowboys** on horseback drive big herds of cattle. The word cowboy is made up of the English words “cow” and “boy”.

abschnitte.titel: From the countryside to the city
abschnitte.text: Many people leave their village and move to the city because they are looking for work, schools or hospitals there. This is called **rural depopulation**. Today, more people in the world live in cities than in the countryside. Some villages become smaller as a result. In Switzerland, however, many families also move from the city to villages nearby.

gewusst: Since about 2007, more people in the world have lived in cities than in the countryside.
Many Swiss municipalities have fewer than 1,000 inhabitants.

teile.einleitung: Lianas are climbing plants that grow upwards on trees. Especially in the tropical rainforest, they hang like long ropes between the trees.
wichtigste: Lianas are climbing plants without a thick trunk of their own to hold them up.
They usually root in the forest floor and climb up towards the light.
Some lianas grow more than 100 metres long.
Monkeys use lianas to climb from tree to tree.
Rattan furniture comes from the climbing rattan palm.
Ivy in Swiss woods is also a liana.

abschnitte.text: **Lianas** are plants that climb up other plants. They have no thick trunk of their own to support them. Instead they use trees as a support. Some wind around the trunk, while others hold on with **tendrils**, thorns or **aerial roots**. Many lianas are woody and can live to a great age.

It is dark on the floor of the rainforest, because the tree crowns block almost all the light. Most lianas **germinate in the forest floor**. From there they climb up a tree until they reach the sun at the top. This saves them the effort of building a strong trunk of their own. Some lianas grow **more than 100 metres** long.

Lianas hang between the trees like ropes. **Monkeys** climb along them and so get from tree to tree. Other animals also use lianas as bridges. Many insects and birds find food and hiding places in them.

The **rattan palm** climbs up trees like a liana. Its flexible stems are woven into baskets and **rattan furniture**. **Vanilla** is also a climbing plant, an orchid whose pods are used as a spice. The **strangler fig** often germinates high up on a tree. Its roots grow downwards and wrap ever more tightly around the tree until it dies.

abschnitte.titel: Lianas in our part of the world
abschnitte.text: Lianas are not found only in the tropics. In Swiss woods grows **ivy**. It climbs up trees and walls with small aerial roots and stays green in winter too. The **clematis** is also a native liana, often seen at the edges of woods.

gewusst: A strangler fig can grow right around a tree until only a hollow sheath of roots is left standing.
Vanilla belongs to the big family of orchids.

teile.einleitung: Malaysia is a country in South-East Asia. It consists of two parts separated by the South China Sea, and it is a special form of monarchy.
wichtigste: Malaysia lies in South-East Asia and consists of two parts.
West Malaysia lies on the Malay Peninsula, East Malaysia in the north of Borneo.
The capital is Kuala Lumpur.
The currency is called the ringgit.
The king is elected by the rulers of nine states.
After Indonesia, Malaysia is the second biggest palm oil producer in the world.

abschnitte.text: **West Malaysia** lies on the **Malay Peninsula** and borders Thailand, and Singapore lies to the south. **East Malaysia** lies in the north of the big island of **Borneo**. In between lies the **South China Sea**. The capital, **Kuala Lumpur**, lies in West Malaysia and is known for the Petronas Towers.

Malaysia is an **elective monarchy**. Nine of its states have rulers of their own, mostly **sultans**. Every five years they choose one of their number to be king. The country is governed by a parliament and a prime minister. In this way Malaysia combines old traditions with a modern government.

In Malaysia people pay with the **ringgit**. An important product is **palm oil**, which is found in food, cosmetics and fuel. After Indonesia, Malaysia produces the most palm oil in the world. Large areas of rainforest were cleared for the **plantations**. This threatens animals such as the **orangutan** on Borneo.

The highest mountain in Malaysia is **Kinabalu** in the state of **Sabah** on Borneo. It is about 4,100 metres high. The national park around the mountain is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. A great many different plants grow there, including rare orchids and pitcher plants.

gewusst: In Malaysia the office of king passes regularly between the rulers of the states.
On Borneo, Malaysia shares the island with Indonesia and the small state of Brunei.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, is an invisible gas without a smell. It is a natural part of the air that plants need to grow. Because humans emit a lot of additional CO2, however, the Earth is warming.
wichtigste: Carbon dioxide consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
It is colourless, odourless and makes up only about 0.04 per cent of the air.
Plants take in CO2, and humans and animals breathe it out.
Before industrialisation the air contained about 280 ppm of CO2, in 2024 over 420 ppm.
CO2 is the most important greenhouse gas caused by humans.
It is produced mainly when coal, oil and natural gas are burned.

abschnitte.text: One particle of **carbon dioxide** consists of one **carbon atom** and two **oxygen atoms**, hence the formula CO2. The gas is colourless, has no smell and is heavier than air. Only very little of it is in the air, about 0.04 per cent. The content is often measured in **ppm**, which means parts per million parts of air.

Plants take CO2 from the air. With sunlight they make sugar from it and give off oxygen. This is called **photosynthesis**. Humans and animals, by contrast, breathe in oxygen and breathe out CO2. The **oceans** also take up a lot of CO2. In doing so, however, they become slightly more acidic, which harms corals, for example.

CO2 lets sunlight through, but holds back part of the heat radiated by the Earth. That is why it is called a **greenhouse gas**. Without greenhouse gases it would be very cold on Earth. But when more and more CO2 is in the air, it gets warmer. CO2 contributes most to **human-caused warming**, because humans emit a great deal of it and it stays in the atmosphere for a very long time.

Around 1750 the air contained about **280 ppm** of CO2. Since **industrialisation**, people have been burning a lot of **coal**, **oil** and **natural gas**. CO2 is produced in the process. A lot of CO2 also gets into the air when forests are cleared. In 2024 the value was over **420 ppm**. On the volcano **Mauna Loa** in Hawaii the CO2 content has been measured exactly since 1958.

The bubbles in mineral water and lemonade are CO2, which in everyday speech is called carbonation (in German “Kohlensäure”, literally “carbonic acid”). Frozen CO2 is called **dry ice**. It is about minus 78 degrees cold and turns directly into gas without first becoming liquid. Fire extinguishers with CO2 smother flames because they displace the oxygen.

gewusst: Dry ice does not melt into a puddle, but turns directly into gas.
The series of measurements from Mauna Loa is called the **Keeling Curve** after its founder.

teile.einleitung: The Korean Demilitarised Zone, DMZ for short, separates North Korea and South Korea. It arose in 1953 with the armistice in the Korean War. To this day there is no peace treaty, and Switzerland too helps to monitor the armistice.
wichtigste: The armistice agreement of the Korean War was signed on 27 July 1953.
A peace treaty was never concluded.
The DMZ runs about 250 kilometres across the Korean Peninsula.
It follows the front line of 1953 and not exactly the 38th parallel.
In Panmunjom, meetings between the two sides still take place to this day.
Switzerland and Sweden have monitored the armistice since 1953.
Because hardly anyone goes in, the DMZ is a refuge for nature.

abschnitte.text: From 1950 to 1953 the **Korean War** raged between North and South Korea, supported by other states. On **27 July 1953** an **armistice agreement** was signed. It ended the fighting. A **peace treaty**, however, was never concluded. Formally there is therefore still no peace between the two states today.

The **Demilitarised Zone** is about **250 kilometres** long. It runs from the mouth of the **Han River** in the west to the east coast. In its middle runs the **Military Demarcation Line**, the actual border. The zone does not follow exactly the 38th parallel, but the **front line** of 1953. “Demilitarised” means that no troops are supposed to be stationed there. On both sides of it, however, the border is very heavily guarded.

In the village of **Panmunjom** on the demarcation line the armistice was signed. There lies the **Joint Security Area**, in which soldiers of both sides stand directly facing each other. In blue huts talks take place. In 2018 the heads of state **Kim Jong-un** from the north and **Moon Jae-in** from the south met here.

The **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission** monitors whether the armistice is being observed. **Switzerland** and **Sweden** are represented on it. Members of the Swiss Armed Forces have been stationed in Panmunjom since 1953. This is one of the oldest peace-support missions of the Swiss Armed Forces.

abschnitte.titel: Dispute at sea and on land
abschnitte.text: The agreement did not settle the **sea border**. In the **Yellow Sea** the UN side drew the **Northern Limit Line**, which North Korea does not recognise. There clashes occurred several times, for example in 2010 at the island of **Yeonpyeong**. Near the border also lay the **Kaesong Industrial Region**. There North Korean employees worked for South Korean firms. South Korea stopped the project in 2016 after a North Korean nuclear test.

gewusst: Because the DMZ has hardly been entered since 1953, rare animals such as cranes live there.
The DMZ is a nature reserve that nobody planned.

teile.einleitung: The Mapuche are an Indigenous people in the south of South America. They are the biggest Indigenous people in Chile and also live in Argentina.
wichtigste: The Mapuche are the biggest Indigenous people in Chile.
They live mainly in the south of Chile and in Argentina.
The name means “people of the earth”.
Their language is called Mapudungun.
They successfully resisted the Spanish conquerors for a long time.

abschnitte.text: The **Mapuche** live mainly in the south of **Chile** and in the west of **Argentina**. Their name means “people of the earth”. The connection to the land and to nature is very important for their culture. Their own language is called **Mapudungun**. Today many Mapuche also live in cities such as Santiago de Chile.

When the **Spanish** conquered Chile in the 16th century, the Mapuche resisted successfully for a long time. Over many generations they were able to keep a large area south of the **Biobío** River independent. Only in the 19th century did the states of Chile and Argentina occupy their land by force.

Many Mapuche today demand that their land and their rights be recognised. This is much debated in Chile, and there are different opinions about it. At the same time, many Mapuche look after their **language**, their music and their festivals so that the culture stays alive.

gewusst: After the arrival of the Spanish, the Mapuche remained independent in a large area for about three centuries.

teile.einleitung: La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia in South America. The city lies at about 3,600 metres above sea level, which makes it the highest seat of government in the world.
wichtigste: La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia.
The city lies at about 3,600 metres in a basin in the Andes.
No other seat of government in the world lies so high.
According to the constitution, the capital is Sucre.
A large cable car network links La Paz with the neighbouring city of El Alto.
The snow-capped mountain Illimani rises above the city.

abschnitte.text: La Paz lies in a deep **basin** in the **Andes**. The houses climb up the steep slopes. The centre lies at about **3,600 metres**, which is higher than almost all the peaks of the Swiss Prealps. Above the city rises the mighty, snow-capped mountain **Illimani**. Above the basin, at about 4,000 metres, lies the large neighbouring city of **El Alto**.

abschnitte.titel: Seat of government, but not the capital
abschnitte.text: Bolivia has a special feature: according to the constitution, **Sucre** is the capital. The highest court sits there. The government and Parliament, however, work in **La Paz**. That is why La Paz is called the **seat of government**. The city was founded in the 16th century by the Spanish. Its name means “peace”.

Because the streets are steep and often jammed with traffic, La Paz has built a large **cable car network**. It is called **Mi Teleférico** and opened in 2014. The colourful lines link the districts in the valley with El Alto. For many people the cable car is now a completely normal way of getting about, just as buses or trams are elsewhere.

At great heights the **air is thinner**. With every breath it contains less oxygen. Many visitors therefore get a headache at first or tire quickly, which is called **altitude sickness**. The body gets used to it after a few days, though. Football teams from the lowlands often struggle in La Paz because they run out of breath more quickly.

gewusst: Lake Titicaca, one of the highest large lakes in the world, lies not far from La Paz.
Mi Teleférico is regarded as one of the biggest urban cable car networks in the world.

teile.einleitung: Lebanon is a small country in the Middle East on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. It is known for its mountains, the cedar and a very long history.
wichtigste: The capital of Lebanon is Beirut.
A green cedar is shown on the flag.
Lebanon is about a quarter as big as Switzerland.
In ancient times the Phoenicians lived on the coast.
The fertile Beqaa Valley lies between two mountain ranges.
Lebanon used to be called the “Switzerland of the Middle East”.

abschnitte.text: Lebanon borders Syria and Israel and lies on the **Mediterranean**. The capital, **Beirut**, lies on the coast and is the country's biggest city. At about 10,450 square kilometres, Lebanon is about **a quarter as big as Switzerland**. The official language is Arabic, and many people also speak French or English.

Running parallel to the coast is the **Mount Lebanon range**, and in the east on the border with Syria the **Anti-Lebanon**. Between the two ranges lies the fertile **Beqaa Valley**. Grain, vegetables and wine are grown there. In winter there is often snow on the mountains, and you can even go skiing there.

The **Lebanon cedar** grows in the mountains and has been a symbol of the country since ancient times. Its wood was already in great demand in antiquity, for example for ships and temples. Today only a few old cedar forests are left. A green cedar can be seen in the middle of the **flag**, between two red stripes.

In ancient times the **Phoenicians** lived on the coast. They were a well-known seafaring and trading people. They founded cities such as **Tyre**, **Sidon** and **Byblos** and traded all around the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians developed an alphabet, from which many other alphabets later arose.

Because of its snowy mountains and the strong **banking centre of Beirut**, Lebanon used to be called the “Switzerland of the Middle East”. Many different **religious communities** live in the country, mainly Muslims and Christians. From 1975 to 1990 the country suffered a **civil war**. There have been political and economic crises again and again since then, too.

gewusst: Byblos in Lebanon is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
The word “Bible” goes back to the name of the city of Byblos, which traded in papyrus.

teile.einleitung: In salmon farming, salmon are not caught in the sea but raised in large farms. A large part of the salmon in our shops comes from such farms.
wichtigste: Most salmon sold in shops come from farms.
The fish farmed most is the Atlantic salmon.
Norway is the biggest salmon producer in the world.
The fish grow up in net pens in the sea, for example in the fjords.
Problems include sea lice and farmed fish that escape.
In Switzerland, too, there is salmon farming in indoor facilities on land.

abschnitte.text: In the wild, salmon live first in **fresh water** and later migrate to the sea. Farming copies this. The young salmon first grow up in tanks of fresh water on land. After that they are moved to large **net pens** in the sea. There they are fed until they are big enough. The fish farmed most is the **Atlantic salmon**.

**Norway** is the biggest salmon producer in the world. In the sheltered **fjords** along its long coast there are countless net pens. The cold, clean seawater suits the salmon well. **Chile**, Scotland and the Faroe Islands also farm a lot of salmon. A large part of it is sold to other countries, including Switzerland.

Farmed salmon are given feed made of fishmeal, fish oil and plants such as soya or rapeseed. Wild salmon eat small **crustaceans** that contain a red pigment. This gives their flesh its typical pink colour. That is why a pigment called **astaxanthin** is also mixed into the feed for farmed fish.

Where many fish live close together, diseases and **sea lice** spread easily. These small crustaceans attach themselves to the skin of the fish. Farmed salmon that escape can mix with wild salmon. In addition, leftover feed and droppings end up in the sea. That is why new kinds of farms are being developed, for example closed tanks. In Switzerland, there has been a salmon farm in indoor facilities on land for some years, for example in the **Grisons**.

gewusst: In the wild, a salmon often finds its way back to spawn in the river where it hatched.
In the past, many wild salmon also lived in the Rhine as far as Basel.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is warming more than the Earth on average. You can see this especially in the glaciers, which are shrinking fast. Experts at MeteoSwiss and the glacier monitoring network GLAMOS observe these changes closely.
wichtigste: According to MeteoSwiss, Switzerland has become about 2.9 °C warmer since pre-industrial times (as of 2025).
Worldwide the warming is about 1.3 °C, so Switzerland is warming about twice as much.
Land areas warm more than oceans.
According to GLAMOS, Swiss glaciers lost about a quarter of their volume between 2015 and 2025.
In 2025 alone, about 3 per cent was lost.

abschnitte.text: According to **MeteoSwiss**, Switzerland has become about **2.9 °C** warmer since **pre-industrial times** (as of 2025). Worldwide the warming is about **1.3 °C**. Switzerland is therefore warming about **twice as much**. One reason is that **land areas** warm more than oceans, and Switzerland lies far from the ocean.

The glacier monitoring network **GLAMOS** measures the Swiss glaciers every year. Between 2015 and 2025 their volume shrank by about **24 per cent**, that is, about **a quarter**. In 2025 alone about 3 per cent was lost. Small glaciers have already disappeared completely, and even large ones such as the **Aletsch Glacier** are getting shorter and shorter.

With the warming there are more **hot days** and less snow at low altitudes. Glaciers are important **water stores** for rivers and hydroelectric power stations. When they disappear, meltwater is missing in summer. In the mountains, soils thaw, which can make rockfalls more likely. The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities are adapting to these changes.

gewusst: In just ten years the Swiss glaciers have lost about a quarter of their ice.
Some series of measurements by MeteoSwiss go back to the year 1864.

teile.einleitung: Hummingbirds are tiny, colourful birds that live only in the Americas. They can stand still in the air and even fly backwards. They include the bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world.
wichtigste: Hummingbirds live wild only in North, Central and South America.
The bee hummingbird from Cuba, at about 5 to 6 centimetres, is the smallest bird in the world.
Hummingbirds drink nectar from flowers and eat small insects.
In hovering flight they stand still in the air, and they can fly backwards.
Small hummingbirds beat their wings many dozens of times a second.
At night they save energy in a state of torpor.

abschnitte.text: There are over 300 species of hummingbird. They live only in the **Americas**, most of them in **South America**. Many have an iridescent plumage in green, blue or red. The smallest is the **bee hummingbird** from Cuba. It is only about 5 to 6 centimetres long and weighs about 2 grams, about as much as a small coin. The biggest is the **giant hummingbird** from the Andes.

Hummingbirds drink sweet **nectar** from flowers. For this they have a long, thin **beak** and a long **tongue** that reaches deep into the flower. For protein they also eat small **insects**. When they drink, pollen sticks to them. In this way they carry it to the next flower and help the plants with **pollination**.

Hummingbirds are flying artists. They can fly forwards, sideways and even **backwards**. In **hovering flight** they move their wings so fast that they stand still in the air in front of a flower. Small hummingbirds beat their wings many dozens of times a second. That is why you can hardly see the wings. The fast beating makes a humming sound, which is why they are called **“hummingbirds”** in English, from “to hum”.

Flying fast takes a great deal of energy. Hummingbirds therefore have to keep drinking during the day. At night they cannot feed. Then they fall into a state of **torpor**. Their body cools down, and heart and breathing slow. In this way they need far less energy until the Sun rises in the morning.

Hummingbirds build small, cup-shaped **nests** from plant fibres, moss and spider webs. The spider webs make the nest stretchy. The females usually lay two tiny white eggs. The eggs of the bee hummingbird are hardly bigger than a pea.

gewusst: A hummingbird’s heart can beat over a thousand times a minute in flight.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can really fly backwards.

teile.einleitung: In coral bleaching, corals lose their colour and turn white. It happens mainly when the sea water becomes too warm. If the heat lasts too long, the corals die.
wichtigste: Corals live together with tiny algae that give them colour and food.
When the water becomes too warm, the corals expel these algae.
Without the algae you can see the white limestone skeleton, and the coral bleaches.
If the heat lasts for a long time, the corals starve and die.
If the heat is only brief, corals can recover.
Because of global warming, coral bleaching is happening more and more often.

abschnitte.text: Reef corals are small animals that build a **limestone skeleton**. In their tissue live tiny **algae**, the **zooxanthellae**. These algae make sugar with sunlight and give part of it to the coral. In return they get a safe home. Both benefit from each other, which is called **symbiosis**. The algae also give the corals their beautiful colours.

If the sea water is too **warm** for a longer time, the partnership goes wrong. The corals expel their coloured algae. Now through the transparent tissue you can see the white **limestone skeleton**. The coral looks as if it had been bleached, hence the name **coral bleaching**. Just one to two degrees above the usual summer temperature can be enough over a few weeks.

A bleached coral is not yet dead. But it has hardly any food left. If the water cools down again soon, the algae can return, and the coral **recovers**. If the heat lasts too long, the coral **starves** and dies. Then other algae grow on the skeleton, and the reef loses its variety. Until a reef has recovered completely it often takes many years.

Because of **global warming** the oceans are getting warmer, and marine heatwaves are happening more often. That is why there are more and more big coral bleaching events. On the **Great Barrier Reef** in Australia, for example, huge areas bleached in 2016 and 2017. The sea also takes up a lot of **CO2** and becomes more acidic as a result. This makes it harder for corals to build their limestone skeleton.

gewusst: Some bleached corals briefly glow in bright colours before they turn white.
Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the sea floor, but are home to a great many marine species.

teile.einleitung: Lavaux is a wine-growing area with steep vineyard terraces on the north shore of Lake Geneva in the canton of Vaud. The landscape is so special that it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Lavaux lies in the canton of Vaud on Lake Geneva.
It stretches for about 30 kilometres between Lausanne and the Vevey and Montreux area.
The first terraces were built in the Middle Ages under monasteries.
The most important grape variety is Chasselas.
Sun, lake and walls are the “three suns”.
Since 2007, Lavaux has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: **Lavaux** lies in the canton of **Vaud** on the north shore of **Lake Geneva**, which is called Lac Léman in French. The vineyards rise steeply from the shore. The area stretches for about 30 kilometres between **Lausanne** and the **Vevey** and **Montreux** area. So that vines can be grown on the steep slopes, countless **terraces** with stone walls were built. In between lie small winegrowing villages such as Cully, Lutry or Saint-Saphorin.

In the Middle Ages the area belonged to **monasteries** of the Benedictines and Cistercians. Under their rule, the first steep terraces were laid out from the **11th and 12th centuries**. For many centuries, winegrowing families have looked after and renewed the walls. That is how the landscape you see today came about. Since **2007**, Lavaux has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

It is said that the grapes in Lavaux are warmed by **three suns**. The first is the real **sun** in the sky. The second is the **lake**, which reflects the sunlight onto the slopes. The third is the **stone walls**, which store heat during the day and give it back in the evening. That is why the grapes ripen especially well here.

The most important grape variety in Lavaux is **Chasselas**, called **Gutedel** in German. It is the typical white wine grape of western Switzerland. A well-known vineyard is the **Dézaley** between Lutry and Saint-Saphorin. Its wines carry the label **Grand Cru**, which is an award for especially good sites. Many visitors walk along paths through the vines and enjoy the view across the lake to the Alps.

gewusst: Small tourist trains run through the vineyards of Lavaux, so you can explore the terraces comfortably.
In Vevey, the big winegrowers' festival, the Fête des Vignerons, takes place about every 20 to 25 years.

teile.einleitung: Lake-effect snow is a weather phenomenon on big lakes in which a great deal of snow can fall in a short time. It is especially well known on the Great Lakes in North America.
wichtigste: “Lake effect” means that the lake itself causes the effect (in German it is called “Seeeffekt”).
Cold air moves across a lake that is still warmer and not frozen.
The air picks up warmth and moisture on the way.
On the downwind shore it snows in strong bands.
The city of Buffalo on Lake Erie, for example, is known for this.

abschnitte.text: In late autumn and early winter, the water of the **Great Lakes** is still warmer than the air. When icy **polar air** then flows over the lake, it picks up **warmth** and **moisture** from below. The moist air rises and cools. Dense clouds form. When they reach the shore, it snows heavily.

abschnitte.titel: Snow bands on the lee shore
abschnitte.text: The snow falls mainly on the **lee shore**, that is, the side that the wind blows towards. On the Great Lakes this is usually the east or south shore. The snow often comes in narrow **bands**. In one place a lot of snow then falls, while a few kilometres away it hardly snows at all. Well known for this are the city of **Buffalo** on Lake Erie and areas east of Lake Ontario.

The effect works only as long as the lake is not frozen over. If it freezes, the moisture is missing and the lake effect stops. Something similar also happens over seas, for example on the west coast of Japan, where cold winds blow across the Sea of Japan. There, too, a great deal of snow falls in some mountains.

gewusst: In November 2014, more than a metre of snow fell in the Buffalo area within a few days.

teile.einleitung: The Congo is a huge river in Central Africa. It is the river with the most water in Africa and the deepest river in the world. It flows in a great arc through the rainforest and empties into the Atlantic.
wichtigste: After the Nile, the Congo is the second longest river in Africa, about 4,400 to 4,700 kilometres long depending on how it is measured.
It carries more water than any other river in Africa.
In some places it is over 200 metres deep, and no river is deeper.
The Congo crosses the Equator twice.
The capital cities Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the river.
It empties into the Atlantic on the west coast of Africa.

abschnitte.text: Depending on how it is measured, the Congo is about 4,400 to 4,700 kilometres long. Only the **Nile** is longer in Africa. But the Congo carries the most water, much more than the Nile. In the world only the **Amazon** has more water. In some places the Congo is over **200 metres deep**. That makes it the **deepest river** in the world.

The Congo flows in a great **arc** through Central Africa. First it flows north, then west and finally south-west. In doing so it crosses the **Equator** twice. Because its basin lies north and south of the Equator, it is always raining somewhere. That is why it carries a lot of water all year round. On the west coast of Africa it empties into the **Atlantic Ocean**.

A large part of the river flows through the **rainforest**, the second biggest on Earth. There it rains a great deal. Many tributaries join the Congo. For people the river is an important **transport route**, because there are only a few roads in the dense forest. On the Congo, boats and barges carry people and goods.

On the Congo there are many **rapids** and waterfalls. At the city of **Kisangani** lie the **Boyoma Falls**. They consist of several steps over about 100 kilometres and used to be called the **Stanley Falls**. Between Kinshasa and the sea too, the river plunges over many rapids. That is why ships cannot sail from the sea deep into the country.

Two countries bear the name of the river: the **Democratic Republic of the Congo** and the **Republic of the Congo**. Their capital cities **Kinshasa** and **Brazzaville** face each other directly across the river. Only the Congo separates them. The broad river is also a border for animals. **Bonobos** live only south of it, because they cannot swim.

gewusst: Apart from Rome and Vatican City, no two capital cities in the world lie as close together as Kinshasa and Brazzaville.
In the deep Congo live species of fish that occur nowhere else.

teile.einleitung: Magma is molten rock deep inside the Earth. When it reaches the surface in a volcanic eruption, it is called lava.
wichtigste: Magma is hot, liquid rock beneath the Earth's surface.
It mostly comes from the mantle beneath the Earth's crust.
Because it is lighter than the rock around it, it rises.
Gases are dissolved in magma, for example water vapour.
At the surface, the molten rock is called lava.
When magma cools slowly deep down, granite, for example, forms.

abschnitte.text: **Magma** is molten rock. It is very hot and therefore liquid, roughly like thick porridge. The word comes from Greek and means “kneaded mass”. Magma forms mainly in the **mantle**, the layer beneath the Earth's crust. It is so hot there that rock can melt.

Hot magma is lighter than the solid rock around it. That is why it slowly rises, rather like an air bubble in water. Beneath many volcanoes it collects in a **magma chamber** a few kilometres down. **Gases** are also dissolved in magma, such as water vapour, just as carbon dioxide is in a bottle of fizzy water.

If too much magma and gas collect beneath a volcano, the pressure keeps growing. At some point the volcano erupts. As soon as the molten rock comes out at the surface, it is called **lava**. Beforehand, researchers often notice that the ground rises slightly and trembles. Instruments show this, so people can be warned in time.

When magma cools, it becomes solid and new rock forms. If it cools very slowly deep in the Earth, large crystals form. This is how **granite**, with its clearly visible grains, is formed. Granite is also found in the **Swiss Alps**, for example in the Gotthard area. If lava solidifies quickly at the surface, the rock becomes fine-grained, as with **basalt**.

gewusst: Granite is solidified magma that never reached the Earth's surface but became visible only through erosion.
Magma and lava are the same material, and only the place decides the name.

teile.einleitung: A lagoon is a shallow body of water on the coast that is separated from the open sea by sandbanks, islands or reefs. Lagoons are important habitats, and some cities have even been built in the middle of a lagoon.
wichtigste: A lagoon is a shallow coastal body of water, largely cut off from the sea.
It is connected to the sea through narrow openings.
The word comes from the Latin “lacuna”, meaning a hollow or pond.
Venice lies in a lagoon that is separated from the Adriatic by the Lido.
The salt content depends greatly on rivers and evaporation.
Lagoons are a sheltered nursery for young fish.
