According to a 2025 report, warm-water coral reefs have passed their tipping point.

abschnitte.text: The British researcher **Timothy Lenton** and his team described in 2008 parts of the climate system that can **tip**. When such an element reaches a critical threshold, the **tipping point**, it changes greatly. A **positive feedback** then reinforces the change by itself. Negative feedbacks, by contrast, would stabilise the system.

Bright ice throws back most of the sunlight, while dark sea water absorbs a lot of it. When sea ice melts, the water warms more, and still more ice melts. This is called the **ice-albedo feedback**. A system that has tipped often returns only at a much lower temperature. This phenomenon is called **hysteresis**.

The **West Antarctic Ice Sheet** is considered especially unstable. It lies on bedrock **below sea level** that gets deeper further inland. Warm sea water can push in under the ice. The **Thwaites Glacier** is often called the “Doomsday Glacier”. It is about as big as Great Britain, and its collapse could raise sea level in the long term by several metres.

The **Atlantic overturning circulation** brings a lot of warmth to the North Atlantic. If it collapsed, it would become markedly colder in **north-western Europe** despite global warming. The **Amazon rainforest** produces part of its own rain through evaporation. Through deforestation and droughts it could change over large areas into a dry **savanna**.

The **Global Tipping Points Report** found in 2025 that **warm-water coral reefs** have already passed their tipping point. Repeated marine heatwaves lead to widespread **coral bleaching**. In it the corals lose their colour and can die. Experts stress that rapid climate protection reduces the risk of further tipping elements.

gewusst: The Thwaites Glacier is roughly as big as Great Britain.
Part of the rain in the Amazon region comes from water that the forest itself evaporates.

teile.einleitung: Laterite is a red, heavily weathered soil or rock material that forms in the hot, humid tropics. It is rich in iron and aluminium but poor in nutrients for plants.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Latin word for brick.
Laterite forms at high temperatures and with a lot of rainfall over a long time.
Iron and aluminium oxides give it its red colour.
Without a cover of plants, it can harden into a hard crust.
Lateritic soils can hardly store any nutrients.
Bauxite, the raw material for aluminium, forms in a similar way.

abschnitte.text: The name **laterite** comes from the Latin word “later”, which means **brick**. Laterite hardens in the air into a material like brick. In **India** and **South-East Asia** it was therefore cut into blocks and used as a building material. Some old temples were also partly built of laterite.

Laterite forms in the **tropics**, where it is very warm for a long time and rains a lot. The warmth speeds up the **chemical weathering** of the rock. The large amount of seeping water washes out easily dissolved substances such as silica. What remains are the **iron and aluminium oxides**, which dissolve only with difficulty. They give the soil its typical **red colour**. Over millions of years, very deep soils form in this way.

Although lush rainforests grow in the tropics, lateritic soils are not very productive for **farming**. Weathering has washed out most of the nutrients. The typical clay mineral **kaolinite** can hold on to only a few nutrients. Under the international soil classification, many such soils belong to the **Ferralsols**. They cover large parts of the Amazon Basin and Central Africa.

If the forest is cleared, the protective cover of plants is gone. Sun and rain hit the soil directly. Then **hard crusts** of laterite can form. These can hardly be worked any more and make farming very difficult. That is why in the tropics it is hard to get good harvests on cleared land for a long time.

**Bauxite** forms through weathering similar to that of laterite. But it is especially rich in **aluminium**. Bauxite is the most important raw material for making aluminium. This is used, for example, to make drinks cans, window frames and parts of aeroplanes.

gewusst: Many rainforest plants get their nutrients mainly from fallen leaves and not from the deep soil.
The red colour of laterite comes from iron oxide, which is also found in rust.

teile.einleitung: Condensation is the process in which water vapour becomes liquid water. It happens when moist air cools down. This is how clouds, fog and the droplets on a cold bottle form.
wichtigste: In condensation a gas such as water vapour becomes liquid again.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
When moist air cools, the vapour condenses into small droplets.
The temperature at which this happens is called the dew point.
This is how clouds, fog and dew form.
The opposite of condensation is evaporation.

abschnitte.text: In the air there is always some invisible **water vapour**. Warm air can take up a lot of it, and cold air less. When moist air cools, it can no longer hold as much water vapour. The vapour then turns into tiny **water droplets**. This process is called **condensation**. The temperature at which it begins is called the **dew point**.

Warm, moist air rises. Up there it is colder, and the air cools. The water vapour **condenses** on tiny dust particles into droplets. Many billions of such droplets form a **cloud**. When the drops become big and heavy enough, they fall to the Earth as **rain**. Condensation is therefore an important part of the **water cycle**.

**Fog** is a cloud right at the ground. It forms when the air near the ground cools strongly, for example on clear autumn nights. In the Swiss **Central Plateau** a thick blanket of fog often lies for days in autumn and winter. **Dew** forms when water vapour condenses on cool blades of grass. In the morning many droplets then glitter on the meadow.

If you take a cold bottle out of the fridge, it soon gets wet. The water vapour from the air condenses on the cold surface. In a similar way, glasses **mist up** when you come in from the cold into a warm room in winter. The bathroom mirror also mists up after a shower. In the sky you see **contrails** behind aeroplanes. There the water vapour from the exhaust gases condenses and freezes.

In **evaporation** liquid water becomes water vapour. This takes heat. In condensation this heat is released again. This **latent heat of condensation** gives thunderstorms and cyclones a great deal of energy.

gewusst: Without dust particles in the air, cloud droplets would form much less easily.
A cloud can contain hundreds of tonnes of water, although it looks light.

teile.einleitung: A cliff is a steep drop at the coast. It forms when the surf strikes the shore again and again and wears away rock. Famous cliffs are found at Dover, on Rügen and in Normandy.
wichtigste: A cliff is a steep slope on the coast shaped by the surf.
At the foot of the cliff the surf washes out a wave-cut notch.
In front of the cliff a flat wave-cut platform is left behind.
A dead cliff is no longer reached by the surf.
Sea stacks are detached towers of rock in the sea.
The cliffs of Dover and Rügen consist of chalk.

abschnitte.text: A **cliff** forms when the **surf** attacks a coast of rock or loose material. The waves knock rock out at the foot of the slope. In this way an indentation forms, the **wave-cut notch**. When the overhang above becomes too big, it breaks off. The cliff thus retreats step by step.

As the cliff retreats, a flat surface of rock is left in front of it. It is called a **wave-cut platform**. The surf has ground it smooth. At low tide it is often visible. When the surf no longer reaches the foot of the cliff, it is called a **dead** or **inactive cliff**. It then gradually becomes overgrown and flatter.

The surf widens cracks in the rock into **caves** and **arches**. At some point a piece of rock is cut off completely. What is left is a free-standing **sea stack**, like the **Lange Anna** (“Long Anna”) on Heligoland. At **Étretat** in Normandy the sea has shaped arches such as the Porte d’Aval. Next to it stands the rock needle L’Aiguille.

The white steep coasts near **Dover** in England and the **Königsstuhl** (“King’s Chair”) on the island of **Rügen** consist of **chalk**. This soft limestone is worn away fairly quickly by the surf. The dissolved material drifts on with the current. On a **coast of equilibrium** it builds up sand spits and **bars** at other places.

gewusst: Chalk consists to a large extent of the tiny limestone shells of sea creatures.
The Lange Anna on Heligoland is about 47 metres high and stands free in the sea.

teile.einleitung: Lagos is the biggest city in Nigeria and one of the biggest cities in Africa. It lies on a lagoon on the Atlantic and is the country's most important centre of business and culture.
wichtigste: Lagos lies on the Lagos Lagoon and on the Bight of Benin.
Until 1991 Lagos was the capital of Nigeria.
The name comes from the Portuguese word for lakes or lagoons.
The Yoruba call the city Eko.
The Third Mainland Bridge is about 12 kilometres long.
Lagos is the centre of the film industry Nollywood.

abschnitte.titel: A city on a lagoon and the sea
abschnitte.text: Lagos lies on the **Lagos Lagoon** and on several islands. The name comes from the **Portuguese** word for lakes or lagoons, because Portuguese sailors gave it to the city. In the language of the **Yoruba** it is called **Eko**. The city lies on the **Bight of Benin**, part of the Gulf of Guinea. A large share of Nigeria's trade passes through its port.

The old trading centre lies on **Lagos Island**, with its harbours and markets. Until **1991**, Lagos was the capital and seat of government of Nigeria. Then the government moved to the newly planned city of **Abuja** in the interior. But Lagos remained the country's biggest city and most important business centre. Many companies and banks have their headquarters here.

The islands are joined to the mainland by bridges. The **Third Mainland Bridge** runs about 12 kilometres across the lagoon and is one of the longest bridges in Africa. A large part of the traffic is carried by the yellow **danfos**. These are private minibuses that run on fixed routes but without an exact timetable. Traffic jams are part of everyday life in Lagos.

In the district of **Makoko**, many houses stand on **stilts** in the lagoon. The people who live there often make their living from fishing and get around in canoes. **Eko Atlantic** is completely different: this new district is being built on sand taken from the sea, and a sea wall keeps the waves out. It is aimed mainly at wealthy residents and companies. So Lagos shows great differences between rich and poor.

**Nollywood** is Nigeria's film industry, and its centre is Lagos. It makes a great many films every year, often quickly and on a small budget. The films are watched all over Africa and beyond. Music from Lagos, such as Afrobeat, is also known worldwide.

gewusst: The name Nollywood is a play on Hollywood in the USA and Bollywood in India.
Lagos is growing so fast that parts of the city are being built on newly reclaimed land.

teile.einleitung: The Congo Rainforest lies in the middle of Africa. After the Amazon rainforest it is the second biggest rainforest on Earth. Gorillas, bonobos, forest elephants and the rare okapi live here.
wichtigste: The Congo Rainforest lies in the middle of Africa.
It is the second biggest rainforest in the world.
It bears the name of the Congo River, which flows right through it.
More than half lies in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Gorillas, bonobos, forest elephants and okapis live here.
The forest is threatened by deforestation.

abschnitte.titel: A forest in the middle of Africa
abschnitte.text: The Congo Rainforest is the biggest rainforest in **Africa**. Only the **Amazon rainforest** in South America is bigger still. That is why the Congo Rainforest is the **second biggest** rainforest on Earth. More than half lies in the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**. Neighbouring countries such as **Cameroon**, **Gabon**, the **Republic of the Congo** and the **Central African Republic** also have a share.

The forest is named after the **Congo** River. It flows right through the rainforest, and many smaller rivers join it. The climate is **hot** and **humid** all year, and it rains a great deal. The trees grow enormously tall. Under their dense canopy it is often dark on the ground.

In the Congo Rainforest live **gorillas**, the biggest great apes. They occur only in Africa. **Chimpanzees** also live here. The **bonobo** lives only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River. Bonobos look very much like chimpanzees and are their closest relatives.

The **okapi** has stripes on its legs like a zebra. Even so, it is a close relative of the **giraffe**. It lives very shyly in the dense forest, and researchers from Europe discovered it only around 1900. **Forest elephants** are smaller than the elephants of the savanna. With their smaller bodies they make their way better in the dense forest.

The rainforest is important for the **climate** of the whole Earth, because its trees store a lot of carbon. But it is threatened. Trees are felled for **valuable timber** and areas are cleared for **fields**. **Poaching** also endangers many animals. **National parks** are meant to protect parts of the forest.

gewusst: The okapi can even clean its own ears with its long tongue.
In the Congo Rainforest there have been peoples for thousands of years who live by hunting and gathering in the forest.

teile.einleitung: Copper is a reddish, shiny metal that people have used for thousands of years. Because it conducts electricity and heat very well, it is found in almost every cable today.
wichtigste: Copper is a chemical element with the symbol Cu.
It conducts electricity and heat very well.
Copper and tin make bronze, and copper and zinc make brass.
In the air, copper slowly forms a green layer called a patina.
Chile has produced the most copper for decades.
Copper can be recycled almost without any loss.

abschnitte.text: Copper is a **chemical element** with the symbol **Cu**. This comes from the Latin word “cuprum”. The name recalls the island of **Cyprus**, where a lot of copper was already mined in ancient times. Copper is soft, bends easily and has a reddish colour. It is one of the few metals that do not look silvery or grey.

Copper **conducts electricity** almost as well as silver, but it is much cheaper. That is why most cables and wires are made of copper. Motors, transformers and computers need it too. Because copper also conducts **heat** well, it is used to make pans and heat exchangers. Electric cars, wind turbines and solar power plants need particularly large amounts of copper.

When metals are mixed, the result is an **alloy**. Copper and tin make **bronze**. It was so important that a whole age is named after it: the **Bronze Age**. Copper and zinc make **brass**, which shines golden yellow and is used for door handles or musical instruments. Many Swiss coins are also made of a mixture of copper and nickel.

Copper is usually taken out of the ground as **ore**. Ore is rock that contains a metal. The country with the biggest copper output is **Chile** (as of 2024). Some of the biggest copper mines in the world lie in the **Atacama Desert**. Old copper can be melted down and used again without becoming any worse. That is why the **recycling** of copper is very valuable.

gewusst: The Statue of Liberty in New York has a skin of copper, and its green colour is a patina.
On copper surfaces, many germs survive for only a short time.

teile.einleitung: Maquiladoras are assembly plants in Mexico. They import components duty-free, put them together and export the finished products, mostly to the USA.
wichtigste: Maquiladoras are assembly plants in Mexico.
They import parts duty-free and export finished products.
Many lie on the border with the USA, for example in Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez.
The programme began in 1965 as the Border Industrialization Program.
NAFTA in 1994 boosted their growth, and in 2020 it was replaced by USMCA.
Low wages and difficult working conditions are criticised.

abschnitte.text: A **maquiladora** is a factory in **Mexico** that puts together imported components. The parts enter the country without **customs duty**, are assembled using cheap labour and exported again as finished products. This principle is called **contract processing**: mainly labour is added in the country. The value added that stays in Mexico is therefore often small.

abschnitte.titel: On the border with the USA
abschnitte.text: Especially many maquiladoras lie on the **border with the USA**. Being close to the big US market saves transport costs and delivery time. In addition, wages in Mexico are clearly lower than in the USA. Cities such as **Tijuana** and **Ciudad Juárez** became big industrial centres in this way.

In 1965 Mexico launched the **Border Industrialization Program**. Before that, the Bracero programme, under which Mexican farm workers had worked in the USA, had come to an end. New jobs were to be created in the border area. In 1994 the free trade agreement **NAFTA** between the USA, Canada and Mexico came into force and cut tariffs. Since 1 July 2020 the **USMCA** has applied instead, with, among other things, stricter rules for cars.

Many maquiladoras work for the **electronics** and **car industries**. They assemble, for example, wiring harnesses, car parts or televisions. Clothes and medical products are also made there. The products go mainly to the North American market.

Supporters stress that maquiladoras have created hundreds of thousands of **jobs**. Critics complain about **low wages**, long working hours and weak trade unions. **Environmental problems** in the quickly grown border area are also mentioned. Opinions about this differ.

gewusst: Tijuana lies directly on the border with the US city of San Diego.
The name maquiladora comes from the Spanish word “maquila”, an old fee that millers charged for grinding grain.

teile.einleitung: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow directly in the sea on tropical coasts. They form dense forests that protect coasts and give many animals a home.
wichtigste: Mangroves grow on tropical coasts where the tides come and go.
They can tolerate salty seawater.
Many mangroves stand on stilt roots in the mud.
Their roots slow down waves and storm surges.
Young fish find shelter among the roots.
Indonesia has the biggest area of mangroves in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Mangroves** are trees and shrubs on tropical coasts. They grow where the **tide ebbs and flows**. At high tide they stand in water, and at low tide in mud. Most trees would die in salt water. Mangroves, however, can tolerate the **salt** well, and some even give it off again through their leaves.

Many mangroves stand on **stilt roots** that rise above the water like legs. This is how they hold on in the soft mud. There is hardly any air in the mud. Some species therefore grow roots that stick up out of the ground and take in air, known as **breathing roots**.

**Young fish** can hide well among the roots, and big predators can hardly get in there. That is why mangroves are also called a nursery of the sea. Special among the animals is the **mudskipper**: this fish can stay on land for a while and hop across the mud on its pectoral fins. In the **Sundarbans** in Bangladesh and India, even the Bengal tiger lives.

The dense roots slow down **waves** and **storm surges**. This means the coast is less damaged in storms. The roots also hold the mud in place, so the land is not washed away so quickly. Even so, many mangrove forests have been cleared, for example for prawn farms or building land.

abschnitte.titel: Seeds that sprout on the tree
abschnitte.text: In some mangroves, the **seeds** already sprout on the tree. An elongated seedling grows, which later drops off. It sticks in the mud or drifts on with the water until it finds a hold and grows. The most mangroves are found in **Indonesia** with its many islands: about a fifth of all the mangroves on Earth grow there.

gewusst: The mudskipper is a fish that can hop across the mud on land.
The Sundarbans are among the biggest mangrove forests on Earth, and tigers live there.

teile.einleitung: A meander is a loop or bend that a river forms. From above, a meandering river looks like a wavy line. Meanders change all the time, because the river wears away one side and deposits material on the other.
wichtigste: A meander is a loop in a river.
The name comes from the river Maiandros in present-day Turkey.
On the outside lies the steep cut bank, where the water wears away the ground.
On the inside lies the gentle slip-off slope with sand and gravel banks.
A loop that has been cut off is called an oxbow lake.
At Saint-Ursanne in the canton of Jura, the Doubs forms a big loop.

abschnitte.text: A **meander** is a bend or loop of a river. Meanders form mainly in flat plains, where the river has little gradient. The name comes from the ancient river **Maiandros** in present-day Turkey, which is now called the Büyük Menderes. It flows in so many loops that all such river bends were named after it. A decorative band in Greek art is also called a meander.

In a bend, the water flows faster on the **outside**. It hits the bank and wears the ground away. That is why the bank becomes steep there, and it is called the **cut bank**. On the **inside** the water flows slowly. Sand and gravel are left lying there, and a gentle bank forms, the **slip-off slope**. In this way the loops move further and further over time.

If the loops become tighter and tighter, only a narrow neck of land is left between them. In a **flood**, the river can break through this neck and take a short cut. The old loop is left behind as an **oxbow lake**. The water in it is almost still. Oxbow lakes are valuable habitats for frogs, dragonflies, fish and waterbirds.

Sometimes a river has cut deep into the rock with its loops. These are called **incised meanders**. A famous example is **Horseshoe Bend** in Arizona in the USA. There the **Colorado River** winds deep in a gorge almost all the way round a rock. From above the loop looks like a horseshoe, hence the name.

In Switzerland, too, there is a well-known big river loop. The **Doubs** comes from France and flows for a stretch into the **canton of Jura**. At **Saint-Ursanne** it makes a wide loop and then returns to France. The landscape inside this loop is called the **Clos du Doubs**. Many Swiss rivers were straightened in the past, and today in some places they are being given more room again.

gewusst: By cutting off meanders, a river can suddenly become shorter in a single flood.
Straightened rivers flow faster, so floods can become stronger downstream.

teile.einleitung: The weather changes from day to day. Climate, by contrast, describes what the weather at a place is mostly like over many years. For climate, people therefore look at measurements over about 30 years.
wichtigste: Climate is the weather over many years.
Climate is mostly determined from data covering about 30 years.
Weather describes a single day or a few days.
A climate diagram shows temperature and precipitation over the year.
Areas with a similar climate are called climate zones.

abschnitte.text: The **weather** is what we experience outside today: sun, rain, wind or snow. It can change quickly. **Climate**, by contrast, describes how the weather at a place **normally** is. “In Ticino the winters are mostly mild” is a statement about climate. “Today it is raining in Bern” is a statement about weather.

To determine the climate you need **long series of measurements**. Experts mostly take the weather data of about **30 years**. From it they calculate averages for temperature, precipitation or sunshine. In Switzerland this is done by **MeteoSwiss** with many measuring stations across the country.

A **climate diagram** shows for every month the average temperature and the precipitation of a place. The temperature is a line, and the precipitation is columns. In this way you can see at a glance when it is warm, cold, wet or dry. With climate diagrams, places can be compared easily.

The Earth is divided into **climate zones**. In each zone the climate is similar. Around the Equator it is hot and often humid, and at the poles very cold. In between lie temperate zones such as Switzerland. A sentence like “In the Sahara it is almost always dry” also describes the climate.

gewusst: A single very cold winter says nothing yet about the climate, and only many years together show it.
Even in little Switzerland there are big differences in climate, for example between Ticino and the high mountains.

teile.einleitung: Land grabbing means, roughly, the seizing of land. It describes how investors buy or lease huge areas of land, often in poorer countries, and the local people are pushed out in the process.
wichtigste: Land grabbing means the large-scale acquisition of land by investors at the expense of local users.
A big wave began with the food price crisis from 2007/2008.
Small farmers often have only customary land rights that are not officially registered.
The Land Matrix database records large land deals worldwide.
In 2012 the UN adopted voluntary guidelines to protect land rights.
Environmental projects can also lead to land seizure, which is called green grabbing.

abschnitte.text: In **land grabbing**, companies, states or funds buy or lease very large areas of land. Often these lie in countries of the **Global South**, that is, poorer countries in Africa, Asia or Latin America. The people who have used the land until then are often **pushed out** without having any say. Supporters of such investments say they bring money, jobs and modern technology. Critics stress that the local population often loses its land and its source of food.

From 2007/2008 the price of grain rose sharply, which is called the **food price crisis**. Countries that have to import a lot of food wanted to secure their supplies. Investors from the **Gulf states** such as Saudi Arabia, where there is not enough water for farming, were particularly active. At the same time, investors were looking for safe ways to put their money, and they discovered **farmland**. This is how a wave of large land deals abroad began.

In 2008 the South Korean company **Daewoo Logistics** wanted to lease about 1.3 million hectares of land in **Madagascar**. Mainly maize and palm oil for South Korea were to be grown there. This set off fierce **protests**. In 2009 they helped to bring down the government, and the deal was then stopped. The case made the issue known all over the world.

In many countries, families have used their land for generations according to **customary law**, that is, according to rules handed down over time. There is often no entry in a **land register**. Formally the land then belongs to the state, which can hand it over to investors. In 2012 the UN adopted the **VGGT guidelines**, which are meant to strengthen such land rights. They are voluntary, however, and not legally binding.

The independent database **Land Matrix** has been collecting information on large land deals of 200 hectares or more since 2012. Among those involved is the Centre for Development and Environment at the **University of Bern**. A newer term is **green grabbing**. It means seizing land for environmental goals, for example for protected areas, tree planting or CO2 offsetting projects, when local people are pushed out as a result.

gewusst: A hectare is a square of 100 by 100 metres, about the size of a football pitch.
1.3 million hectares is almost a third of the area of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Martinique is an island in the Caribbean. It belongs to France and therefore also to the European Union, even though it lies far away from Europe.
wichtigste: Martinique lies in the Caribbean, in the Lesser Antilles.
The island is an overseas territory of France.
It belongs to the European Union.
People pay with the euro.
The capital is called Fort-de-France.

abschnitte.text: **Martinique** lies in the eastern **Caribbean** and belongs to the **Lesser Antilles**. The island is mountainous and of volcanic origin. Its highest mountain is the volcano **Montagne Pelée**. The climate is tropical and warm all year round. The capital is called **Fort-de-France**.

Martinique is an **overseas territory of France**. The people are French citizens, and the official language is French. People also speak **Creole**. Because Martinique belongs to France, the island is also part of the **European Union**. That is why people there pay with the **euro**.
**Bananas** and **sugar cane** are grown in Martinique. Rum is made from sugar cane. **Tourism** is also important, and many guests come for the beaches and the nature.

gewusst: Although Martinique lies in the Caribbean, the island belongs to the EU and people pay with euros.
In 1902 an eruption of the Montagne Pelée destroyed the then capital, Saint-Pierre.

teile.einleitung: Lake St Clair is a smaller lake in North America between Lake Huron and Lake Erie. It is not counted among the five Great Lakes, but it is an important link between them.
wichtigste: Lake St Clair lies between Lake Huron and Lake Erie.
It is not one of the five Great Lakes.
The water arrives via the St Clair River and flows on via the Detroit River.
The lake is only a few metres deep.
The border between the USA and Canada runs through it.

abschnitte.titel: A lake between the Great Lakes
abschnitte.text: **Lake St Clair** lies between **Lake Huron** to the north and **Lake Erie** to the south. The water of Lake Huron flows into the lake via the **St Clair River**. From there it flows on into Lake Erie via the **Detroit River**. The border between the US state of **Michigan** and the Canadian province of **Ontario** runs right through the lake. On its south-west shore lies the big city of **Detroit**.

At about 1,100 km², Lake St Clair is roughly twice as big as Lake Constance, but only **a few metres deep**. For the big cargo ships on the Great Lakes, a deeper **shipping channel** was therefore dredged. Ships sail through it from Lake Huron to Lake Erie and beyond. Because it is so small compared with its neighbours, it is not counted among the five Great Lakes.

French explorers reached the lake in the 17th century on the feast day of Saint **Clare**. That is why it is called St Clair in English. Today the lake is popular with anglers, sailors and water sports fans.

gewusst: Lake St Clair is sometimes jokingly called the “sixth Great Lake”.

teile.einleitung: Los Angeles is a huge city on the Pacific coast in the south of California. It is the second biggest city in the USA and world famous for Hollywood and the film industry.
wichtigste: Los Angeles lies in the state of California.
The name is Spanish and means “the angels”.
The Spanish founded the city in 1781.
After New York City, Los Angeles is the second biggest city in the USA.
The city hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984, and will do so again in 2028.
Earthquakes and smog are well-known problems of the city.

abschnitte.text: Los Angeles lies in the south of **California** on the **Pacific**. The Spanish name means **“the angels”**, and people often just say **L.A.** The Spanish founded the settlement in **1781**. Later the area belonged to Mexico, and from 1848 to the USA. In the 2020 census the city had almost **3.9 million** inhabitants, making it the second biggest city in the USA after New York City. In third place comes Chicago.

In the district of **Hollywood**, many film studios were set up at the start of the 20th century. The sunny weather made it possible to film outdoors all year round. Today Hollywood is a name for the whole American film industry. Well known are the big **Hollywood sign** on a hill and the stars of famous people in the pavement.

Los Angeles has a **Mediterranean climate**: warm, dry summers and mild winters, when most of the rain falls. The city lies in a **basin** surrounded by mountains. The mountains trap the exhaust fumes from the heavy traffic. In sunshine, **smog** forms from them. In dry periods there are often forest fires in the surrounding area.

The **San Andreas Fault** runs close by. There, two **tectonic plates**, the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate, rub against each other. This causes **earthquakes** again and again. Houses and bridges are therefore built to be especially earthquake-proof.

Los Angeles hosted the **Summer Olympics** in 1932 and 1984. In 2028 the Games will take place there again. That will make Los Angeles an Olympic city **three times**. The city also has one of the biggest ports in the USA and one of the busiest airports in the world.

gewusst: The Hollywood sign originally read “Hollywoodland” and was an advertisement for a housing development.
The full Spanish name under which the city was founded was much longer than “Los Angeles”.

teile.einleitung: Krakatoa is a volcanic island in Indonesia between Java and Sumatra. In August 1883 the volcano exploded in one of the most violent eruptions of modern times. The bang could be heard thousands of kilometres away, and huge tidal waves destroyed many coastal villages.
wichtigste: Krakatoa lies in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra in Indonesia.
The eruption reached its peak on 26 and 27 August 1883.
The greatest part of the island vanished in the explosion.
About 36,000 people died, most of them through tsunamis.
The bang could be heard almost 5,000 kilometres away.
The eruption reached level 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index.
Since 1927 the new volcano Anak Krakatau has been growing in the same place.

abschnitte.text: Krakatoa lies in the **Sunda Strait**, the strait between the islands of **Java** and **Sumatra**. It belongs to **Indonesia**, a country with a great many active volcanoes. The reason is its position on a plate boundary. There one plate of the Earth dives beneath another, and magma forms.

Already months earlier the volcano was restless. On **26 and 27 August 1883** the most violent explosions occurred. The biggest took place on the morning of **27 August**. The volcano hurled out about 20 cubic kilometres of rock and ash. On the **Volcanic Explosivity Index**, VEI for short, it reached level **6**. The greatest part of the island vanished, and a huge **caldera** under the sea was left.

The explosions triggered huge tidal waves, so-called **tsunamis**. They destroyed many villages on the coasts of **Java** and **Sumatra**. Officially over **36,000 deaths** were counted. Most of them died through the tsunamis and not directly from the volcano. It was one of the worst natural disasters of modern times.

The bang could still be heard on the island of **Rodrigues** in the Indian Ocean, almost 5,000 kilometres away. It is regarded as one of the **loudest sounds** in history. Fine **ash** and **sulphur gases** spread through the high atmosphere around the whole Earth. For months they coloured the **sunsets** a striking red. The climate cooled slightly afterwards.

From **1927** a new volcano grew out of the sea in the same place. The locals called it **Anak Krakatau**, in Indonesian “child of Krakatoa”. It is still active today. At the end of 2018 part of its flank slid into the sea and again triggered a tsunami.

gewusst: The pressure wave of the explosion travelled several times around the whole Earth and was measured at weather stations.
In Europe too, the evening skies glowed red for months after the eruption.

teile.einleitung: Continental drift is the idea that the continents move slowly over the Earth. The German researcher Alfred Wegener presented this theory in 1912. At the time many people laughed at him, but today we know that he was right.
wichtigste: Alfred Wegener presented the theory of continental drift in 1912.
Once almost all the land masses formed a supercontinent called Pangaea.
Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago.
In the process the southern continent Gondwana separated from the northern part, Laurasia.
Fossils of Mesosaurus in Africa and South America supported Wegener’s theory.
Symmetrical magnetic stripes on the sea floor prove seafloor spreading.
The Atlantic opens by a few centimetres every year.

abschnitte.text: **Alfred Wegener** (1880 to 1930) was a German meteorologist and polar explorer. He noticed that the coasts of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle. In 1912 he presented his theory that the continents move. He died in 1930 on an expedition in the ice of Greenland, long before his idea was accepted.

At the end of the Palaeozoic, about 300 million years ago, almost all the land masses formed a single supercontinent: **Pangaea**, which means roughly “all the Earth”. Around it lay a huge primeval ocean. About 200 million years ago Pangaea began to break up. First the northern part, **Laurasia**, and the southern part, **Gondwana**, separated, and later these too broke into today’s continents.

Wegener collected much evidence. Fossils of the small freshwater reptile **Mesosaurus** are found in both Africa and South America, although it could never have swum across an ocean. Layers of the same rock and mountain ranges also continue on both sides of the Atlantic. In addition, traces of glaciers were found in regions that are hot today, for example in India and Africa.

Most researchers at first rejected Wegener’s idea. He could not explain what force was supposed to move such huge continents. People imagined that they would have to plough through the solid ocean floor like ships. Only decades after his death was the solution found.

abschnitte.titel: The proof on the sea floor
abschnitte.text: In the 1950s and 1960s the sea floor was studied more closely. In the process the **mid-ocean ridges** were discovered, long mountain ranges under water where new ocean floor is constantly formed. On both sides of them lie symmetrical stripes with different magnetisation, like the annual rings of a tree. They prove **seafloor spreading**, and from this the theory of plate tectonics arose.

The continents are still moving today, at roughly the speed at which our fingernails grow. The Atlantic gets a few centimetres wider every year, so Europe and America are moving away from each other. With satellites and GPS these movements can now be measured exactly. In many millions of years the Earth will therefore look quite different again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A giant continent that unites almost all the land masses of the Earth.
A petrified remnant or imprint of a living thing from primeval times.
The moving apart of the sea floor at the mid-ocean ridges, where new floor forms.
The southern great continent from which South America, Africa, Australia, Antarctica and India arose.

gewusst: Wegener was really a weather researcher and not a geologist.
In Iceland you can walk through a rift between the North American and the Eurasian plates.
India used to be an island and collided with Asia only later.

teile.einleitung: Coal is a black or brown rock that burns. It arose from plants that lived millions of years ago. Coal supplied the energy for industrialisation and is still an important, but climate-damaging, fuel today.
wichtigste: Coal is a fossil fuel that arose from ancient plant remains.
A distinction is made mainly between brown coal (lignite) and the older, harder hard coal.
By far the most coal is mined in China, more than half of the world’s.
A large part of the coal is burned in power stations to make electricity.
For each unit of energy produced, coal releases more CO2 than oil or natural gas.
In Switzerland coal plays hardly any part today.

abschnitte.text: Many millions of years ago huge swamp forests grew. Dead plants sank into the water and could not rot away completely. First **peat** formed. Sand and mud were deposited above it. Through pressure and heat deep down, it turned over a very long time into **brown coal**, then **hard coal** and finally **anthracite**. The older the coal, the more carbon it contains.

With **industrialisation**, coal became very important in the 18th and 19th centuries. It drove **steam engines**, locomotives and factories. Coal is also used to make **coke**, which is needed for making iron and steel. Today coal is burned mainly in **coal-fired power stations** to generate electricity. It is mined in underground mines or in large **open-cast mines**.

**China** is the biggest coal producer in the world and mines more than half of the world’s coal. **India**, **Indonesia**, the **USA** and **Australia** also mine a lot of coal. In many countries coal is cheap and easily available. That is why it is still an important source of electricity there.

Coal consists almost entirely of **carbon**. When it burns, the carbon combines with oxygen to form **carbon dioxide**, CO2 for short. For each amount of energy produced, markedly more CO2 is released than with natural gas. Coal is therefore regarded as the most climate-damaging fossil fuel. In addition, fine dust and other pollutants are produced. Many countries therefore want to phase out coal.

Switzerland has only small coal deposits. In times of need, for example during the two world wars, coal was nevertheless mined. One example is the brown coal mine of **Käpfnach** near Horgen on Lake Zurich, which is now a museum. There is no electricity from coal-fired power stations in Switzerland.

gewusst: Sometimes fossilised imprints of ferns and leaves can be found in coal.
Diamonds and coal both consist almost entirely of carbon.

teile.einleitung: La Niña is a weather phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean in which the sea in the east is especially cool. It is the counterpart of El Niño and affects the weather in many parts of the world.
wichtigste: La Niña is the counterpart of El Niño.
The name is Spanish and means “the girl”.
During it, the water in the eastern Pacific is colder than normal.
In South-East Asia and Australia it then often rains more.
La Niña occurs every few years and can last one to two years.

abschnitte.text: Over the tropical **Pacific**, the **trade winds** normally blow from east to west. They push warm surface water towards South-East Asia. In return, cold water rises from the depths off the coast of South America. During **La Niña** these winds are stronger than usual. As a result, the water in the eastern Pacific becomes **even colder than normal**.

**El Niño** means “the Christ Child” or “the boy” in Spanish. During it, the eastern Pacific is unusually warm. **La Niña** means “the girl” and is the opposite. Both belong to an interplay between sea and air that experts call **ENSO**. Between the two states there are also neutral years.

During La Niña it often rains more than usual in **South-East Asia** and **Australia**, sometimes with floods. On the west coast of South America, on the other hand, it is often drier. Because the Pacific is so big, La Niña affects the weather all over the Earth. Years with La Niña are usually a little cooler worldwide than years with El Niño.

gewusst: From 2020 to 2023 there was La Niña for three years in a row, which is rare.
The cold, nutrient-rich water off Peru is good for fishing.

teile.einleitung: Luke Howard was an English pharmacist who studied the weather in his free time. He gave clouds the Latin names that are still used all over the world today.
wichtigste: Luke Howard lived in England from 1772 to 1864.
By profession he was a pharmacist, and he studied the weather as a hobby.
Around 1802 he classified clouds by their shape.
He used Latin names such as cirrus, cumulus and stratus.
His classification is the basis of today's cloud classification.

abschnitte.text: In the past, clouds had no standard names. In a lecture in London around **1802**, **Luke Howard** presented a classification. He distinguished clouds by their shape and gave them **Latin names**: **cirrus** for wispy clouds, **cumulus** for heap clouds and **stratus** for layer clouds. For rain clouds he used **nimbus**. These names could be understood in every country.

Howard noticed that cloud forms blend into one another. So he combined the names, for example **cirrostratus** or **cumulonimbus** for the big thunderclouds. Today's **cloud classification** of the World Meteorological Organization is built on his system. The **weather report** in Switzerland also uses these terms.

Howard's work quickly became known. The German poet **Johann Wolfgang von Goethe** was enthusiastic and wrote poems about his theory of clouds. Howard also studied the climate of **London** and found that it was warmer in the city than in the countryside.

gewusst: Howard was not a trained scientist but an enthusiastic amateur researcher.
The Latin word “cumulus” means heap.

teile.einleitung: Lee is the side of a mountain range or an object that faces away from the wind. The opposite is called windward, the side that the wind hits.
wichtigste: Lee is the side facing away from the wind, windward is the side facing the wind.
On the windward side the air rises and the rain falls out of it.
On the lee side the air sinks and becomes drier.
This creates a rain shadow, for example in the inner Valais.
The foehn is also a wind on the lee side of the Alps.

abschnitte.text: The words **windward** and **lee** come from seafaring. Windward is the side the wind comes from. Lee is the side that lies in the shelter of the wind. The terms are used for ships, islands, houses and above all for **mountain ranges**.

When moist air meets a mountain range, it has to rise on the windward side. As it does, it cools, clouds form and it rains. On the **lee side** the air sinks again and warms up. It is now drier, so less rain or snow falls there. This dry area is called a **rain shadow**. One example is the **inner Valais**, which is surrounded by high mountains and is therefore one of the driest areas in Switzerland.

The **foehn** is a warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of the Alps. In a south foehn it rains in Ticino, while in the valleys north of the Alps it is warm and clear. The sinking air warms up strongly. In Switzerland the foehn is especially well known in the Reuss valley in Uri and in the Rhine valley.

gewusst: Thanks to the dry climate, even vines and apricots grow well in the Valais.
Sailors talk about “lee” and “windward” to name the sides of their boat.

teile.einleitung: A compass is a device that shows where north is. Its needle is a small magnet that aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field. With a compass you can find your way in the woods, in the mountains and at sea.
wichtigste: A compass shows where north is, and from that you can find all the compass directions.
The compass needle is a small magnet.
The red tip usually points north, and the other end points south.
You must hold the compass flat so that the needle can turn freely.
Magnets and iron nearby interfere with the compass.
The compass was invented in ancient China.

abschnitte.text: The needle of a compass is **magnetic**. The Earth is like a giant **magnet** with a **magnetic field**. This field aligns the needle in a **north-south direction**. On most compasses the tip that points north is **red**. The other end points **south**. If you know north, you can also work out east and west.

A compass is held **flat** in the hand. Only then can the needle turn freely. If it is tilted, the needle sticks. It is also important that there is no **magnet** and no **iron** nearby. Even a mobile phone, a pocket knife or an iron fence can deflect the needle. Then the compass shows a wrong direction.

On many compasses and maps you can see a star with the compass directions. It is called the **compass rose**. On it are **north**, **east**, **south** and **west**, and often the directions in between, such as north-east. Good compasses also have a scale in **degrees**. In this way a direction can be given quite exactly.

The first compasses were in ancient **China**. Later sailors brought the idea to **Europe**. For **seafaring** the compass was very important. On the open sea you often see no land, and in cloud no stars either. With the compass sailors could still keep their heading. Today there is GPS, but a compass also works without electricity and without reception.

In **orienteering** you run through the woods with a map and compass. You have to find certain **control points** in the terrain as quickly as possible. In **Switzerland** orienteering is very popular, and many schools hold orienteering runs. When hiking in the mountains too, a compass helps when fog rolls in.

gewusst: The magnetic North Pole is not exactly at the geographic North Pole, so a compass points slightly to one side of true north.
Swiss runners are among the best in the world at orienteering.

teile.einleitung: A cruise ship is a large passenger ship on which people go on holiday. It sails from port to port, and on board there is almost everything you can also find on land.
wichtigste: A cruise ship is often compared with a floating hotel.
The rooms on a ship are called cabins.
Port is on the left and starboard is on the right when you look forward.
The front is the bow, the back is the stern, and the floors are called decks.
Lifeboats on the side can take in everyone on board in an emergency.
On the Rhine, river cruise ships sail from Basel to the North Sea.

abschnitte.text: On a cruise ship there are **cabins** for sleeping, restaurants, swimming pools, theatres and shops. The guests live on board for the whole trip. During the day the ship often docks in a port, and the guests visit the town. At night it sails on to the next destination. The biggest ships have room for several thousand guests and need a large crew to look after them.

Ships have their own words. The left side is called **port**, the right side **starboard**. This way there is no mix-up, no matter which direction someone is looking in. The front part is the **bow**, the back part the **stern**. The floors are called **decks**, and round, watertight windows are called **portholes**.

**Lifeboats** hang on the sides of a cruise ship. In an emergency, everyone can leave the ship in them. That is why there is a **lifeboat drill** at the start of every trip. In it, all the guests learn where their assembly point is and where the life jackets are kept.

Not all cruise ships sail on the sea. **River cruise ships** are long, narrow and low so that they can pass under bridges. Many trips begin in **Basel** on the **Rhine**. The river flows through Germany and France to the Netherlands and the North Sea. Such ships also sail on the Danube or the Nile.

Big cruise ships bring thousands of people into a town all at once. In popular places it then gets very crowded. Many ships burn **heavy fuel oil** and give off a lot of exhaust fumes even in port. That is why there are new solutions: some ports offer **shore power**, so that the engines can be switched off during a stop. Some cities also limit the number of ships.

gewusst: In 2021, Venice banned large cruise ships from sailing through the city centre.
On many big cruise ships, people from dozens of different countries work together.

teile.einleitung: The legend is the key to a map. It shows what the colours, lines and symbols on the map mean, and so helps you to read a map correctly.
wichtigste: The legend explains the colours, lines and signs of a map.
The simplified map signs are called symbols.
Lakes and rivers are almost always blue on maps.
On Swiss national maps, woods are green areas.
Borders are often drawn with dash-dot lines.
Every map has its own signs, so you read the legend first.

abschnitte.text: A map shows the world greatly reduced and simplified. That is why things such as houses, roads or woods are shown with signs. The **legend** explains these signs. It is also called the **key**. Without a legend you would have to guess what the colours and symbols mean.

The fixed map signs are called **symbols**. There are, for example, signs for a church, a railway station or a viewpoint. Some symbols are little pictures, others are lines or areas. On overview maps, **places** are often drawn as dots or circles, and bigger circles usually stand for bigger cities.

Many colours have become standard. **Bodies of water** such as lakes and rivers are almost always **blue**. On the **national maps of swisstopo**, the Federal Office of Topography, woods are **green areas**. Height maps often show low land as green and high land as brown or white. Exactly which colour means what is always stated in the legend.

Lines, too, have different meanings. Roads, railway lines and paths are drawn differently. The **borders** of countries or cantons are often drawn with **dash-dot lines**. There is, however, no single sign language for maps that applies all over the world. That is why it is important to look at the legend first on every new map.

gewusst: The word “legend” comes from the Latin “legenda” and means “that which is to be read”.
Swiss national maps are regarded internationally as especially accurate and beautifully drawn.

teile.einleitung: At a convergent plate boundary two plates of the Earth move towards each other. Often one plate dives beneath the other, or two continents collide. This produces deep-sea trenches, volcanoes, earthquakes and high mountain ranges such as the Andes, the Himalayas and the Alps.
wichtigste: At convergent plate boundaries two plates move towards each other.
The denser oceanic plate dives beneath the lighter one, which is called subduction.
In front of every subduction zone lies a deep-sea trench, and the deepest is the Mariana Trench.
Water from the sinking plate makes the mantle above it melt, and so volcanoes form.
When an oceanic plate dives beneath an oceanic plate, a volcanic island arc forms.
When two continents collide, mountain ranges such as the Himalayas or the Alps fold up.
Slab pull is regarded as the most important driving force of plate tectonics.

abschnitte.text: When an **oceanic** plate meets a **continental** one, the oceanic one dives down. It consists mainly of **basalt** and has a higher **density** than the lighter continental crust. That is why it sinks into the **Earth’s mantle**. This process is called **subduction**. The cold, heavy plate pulls the rest of the plate along behind it. This **slab pull** is regarded as the most important driving force of plate movement.

Where the plate bends downwards, a long, very deep **deep-sea trench** forms on the sea floor. The deepest is the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific. Its **Challenger Deep** lies almost 11,000 metres below sea level. Sediments on the sinking plate are scraped off at the upper plate and stacked in a wedge shape. This body is called an **accretionary wedge**. In this way the edge of the continent grows over time.

The sinking plate releases **water** at depth. It rises into the mantle above and there lowers the **melting point** of the rock. In this way **magma** forms, which rises and builds volcanoes. On the west coast of South America, the volcanoes of the **Andes** formed like this. When an oceanic plate dives beneath another oceanic plate, an arc-shaped chain of volcanic islands forms, an **island arc**. Examples are the **Marianas** and the **Lesser Antilles**.

At subduction zones there are many and often very strong **earthquakes**. Their foci follow the sinking plate obliquely downwards, to depths of about 700 kilometres. This zone is called the **Wadati-Benioff zone**, after the researchers Kiyoo Wadati and Hugo Benioff. At depth, under high pressure and at a relatively low temperature, special rocks form. One example is **blueschist**, whose colour comes from the mineral **glaucophane**.

Continental crust is too light to dive deep. When two **continents** collide, the rock is compressed, folded and pushed on top of itself. This is how the **Himalayas** formed, when India collided with Asia. The **Alps** also formed in this way: the African Plate and smaller plates moved towards Europe. That is why in the Swiss Alps you find rocks that once lay on the sea floor.

gewusst: The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is high.
Around the Pacific there are so many subduction zones that people speak of the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.

teile.einleitung: There are rivers on every inhabited continent. The longest of them flow for thousands of kilometres, through many countries or right across a whole continent to the sea.
wichtigste: The Nile and the Amazon are the longest rivers on Earth.
At about 6,300 km, the Yangtze in China is the longest river in Asia.
At about 6,000 km, the Mississippi-Missouri system is the longest in North America.
In Europe the Volga is the longest, followed by the Danube.
The Loire is the longest river in France.
The Ob, Yenisei and Lena flow into the Arctic Ocean.

abschnitte.text: The two longest rivers in the world are the **Nile** in Africa and the **Amazon** in South America. Which one is longer depends on where you measure the source. In third place comes the **Yangtze**, at about 6,300 km. It is the longest river in **Asia** and flows only through **China**.

If you measure the **Mississippi** together with its long headwater, the **Missouri**, the total comes to about 6,000 km. This river system is the longest in **North America** and flows into the Gulf of Mexico. The longest river in **Canada** is the **Mackenzie**. It flows about 1,700 km north from Great Slave Lake to the Arctic Ocean. With its headwaters, the system is more than 4,000 km long.

The longest river in Europe is the **Volga** in Russia. In second place comes the **Danube**, at about 2,850 km. It flows through ten countries and into the **Black Sea**. The longest river in **France** is the **Loire**, at about 1,000 km. It flows entirely within France and enters the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire. The **Rhine**, which rises in Switzerland, is about 1,230 km long.

Three huge rivers flow through **Siberia**: the **Ob**, the **Yenisei** and the **Lena**. They flow from south to north and enter the **Arctic Ocean**. For many months of the year they are frozen. In spring, the ice in the south thaws earlier than in the north, so there are often ice jams and floods.

gewusst: The Danube flows through more countries than any other river in the world.
The Rhine and the Rhône both rise in the Gotthard region of Switzerland, not far from each other.

teile.einleitung: The Colosseum in Rome is the biggest amphitheatre that the ancient Romans built. Nearly 2,000 years ago tens of thousands of people gathered here for gladiator fights and animal hunts. Today it is one of the most famous buildings in the world.
wichtigste: The Colosseum stands in Rome and was inaugurated in AD 80.
It had room for about 50,000 spectators and had 80 entrances.
The outer wall is made of travertine, a light limestone.
The name probably comes from a giant statue of Emperor Nero, the “colossus”.
Earthquakes and stone robbing destroyed part of the outer wall.
In 2007 the Colosseum was voted one of the new seven wonders of the world.

abschnitte.text: Emperor **Vespasian** had the Colosseum built around AD 72. His son **Titus** inaugurated it in AD 80. Its real name is the **Amphitheatrum Flavium**, after the imperial family of the Flavians. The name Colosseum probably comes from a giant statue, a **“colossus”** of Emperor **Nero**, that stood next to it. The outer wall is made of **travertine**, a light limestone from near Tivoli. The blocks were held together with iron clamps.

All round there were **80 entrances** with arches. In this way the many spectators could get in and out quickly. Who sat where depended on rank in society. The important people sat at the bottom, close to the arena. Right at the top sat the **poorer people**. Against sun and rain a huge awning could be stretched over the seating.

In the Colosseum **gladiator fights** and hunts of wild animals took place. The floor of the arena was covered with **sand** so that the fighters did not slip. The Latin word **“arena”** means sand. Under the floor lay a maze of passages and rooms, the **hypogeum**. There animals and fighters waited, and by lifts they came up into the arena.

After the end of the Roman Empire the Colosseum was no longer used for games. **Earthquakes** brought parts of the wall down. Later people took the stones to build other buildings in Rome. That is why part of the outer wall is missing today. What is left is carefully looked after and restored.

The Colosseum is one of the most visited buildings in Italy. In 2007, in a worldwide vote, it was chosen as one of the **new seven wonders of the world**. On **Good Friday** a **Way of the Cross** is traditionally prayed at the Colosseum, usually together with the Pope. Italy also shows the Colosseum on its **5-cent coin**.

gewusst: Under the arena floor there were lifts with which animals could suddenly appear in the arena.
The Colosseum is about 48 metres high, about as high as a house with 15 storeys.
